MOTION FOR PRINTING OF EVIDENCE TAKEN BEFORE COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE AND COLONIZATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to move, seconded by Mr. Coote:
That twenty thousand copies in English and five thousand copies in French of the evidence taken by the select standing committee on agriculture and colonization on the consideration of the subject of the grading and inspection of wheat be printed in blue book form, and that distribution be made thereof free of charge by the Department of Trade and Commerce, and that standing order 64 be suspended in relation thereto.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not rise to object to the putting out of the evidence if the agricultural committee determined that its distribution is worth while; but I submit that we are introducing a precedent that later on may, to say the least, create embarrassment and add materially to the expense of carrying on the affairs of this parliament. I have no recollection of parliament ordering the printing of

Grading of Wheat
twenty thousand copies of evidence. It is customary to order the printing of a reasonable amount of such information as is desirable for members of both houses and for distribution to their constituents. But if it is necessary to print this number of copies, why should it not be done by the department interested? The proper procedure, it seems to me, is for the Department of Trade and Commerce, to which we give a considerable vote for printing, to take the responsibility of putting out this evidence, if it is considered worth while to do so. If I understand the motion rightly, Mr. Speaker, it is questionable whether it is an order on the Department of Trade and Commerce to do this work. If it is,
I doubt if a private member has the right to move such a motion.

That twenty thousand copies in English and five thousand copies in French of the evidence taken by the select standing committee on agriculture and colonization on the consideration of the subject of the grading and inspection of wheat be printed in blue book form and that distribution be made thereof free of charge by the Department of Trade and Commerce and that standing order 64 be suspended in relation thereto.

I am not much worried about that so long as we get the printing done. I desire to point out that we have been dealing with a question on which very little information is available in printed form. It is related to an agitation that has extended over the last twenty years; during all that time our farmers have been asking that their wheat should be graded according to its milling value. Your committee went very fully into this matter, and took the evidence of witnesses who are experts in their particular lines, and the information so brought together will be of very great value to the Western farmers.
Now, twenty thousand copies may seem a large number, but with fifty-four constituencies in western Canada, practically all of which will be keenly interested in this question-as I will show in a moment-it means a very small number of copies to each constituency; further, it means that there will be about only one copy for every seven or eight thousand farmers. Some time ago when the evidence was completed, but before the report was issued, I took the trouble to secure from the printing bureau a statement of the cost involved. It did not include the report, nor did it provide for the translation into French. It amounted to only a little more than eight cents a copy. Making allowance for the translation and including the report- 'this resolution does not provide for it but I hope it will be included-the cost would amount to only ten cents a copy. When we consider that the information deals with a subject of great interest to western Canada, I think it is reasonable to expect that all those copies will be ordered.
I hold in my hand half a dozen letters from farmers who, having seen by the press that this matter was discussed in this house, of their own accord wrote for further information. One asks for a dozen copies, another, the secretary of an organization, asked for a dozen copies of the discussion which took place in the house on this subject some months ago, and so on. I have received probably a dozen letters, showing that the fanners are keenly interested in this matter. I believe other members have had the same experience. I do not think I have discussed in this house any question about which I have received so many inquiries, and which seems to have created so much interest. The evidence is quite complete, but unless that information is made available to the farmers so that they may have a chance to study and apply it I am afraid a large part of the benefit of the committee's work will be lost. I

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
I desire to move in amendment:
That all the words after the word "that" in the motion be left out and the following substituted therefor:
"This house is of opinion that the expenditures for the year ending March 31, 1928, and the proposed expenditures for the year ending March 31, 1929, are excessive and extravagant, and that the country has not received, and cannot expect to receive, any adequate returns therefrom."
Mr. Speaker, I offer no apologies for moving this motion at this time. Those members of the house who have the main estimates before them will observe that we voted $366,071,314.22 for the public service last year, in addition to certain supplementary estimates. This year again, however, although we voted these very large sums of money
which were essential to take care of the demands made by the public service, the extravagant demands in my judgment, we were asked to vote a further sum of $7,777,747.89 in two supplementary estimates embodied in Bill No. 155 already passed by this house. So our expenditures, which we thought to be large when we passed the estimates last year, in fact have been swollen not only by supplementary estimates passed last year but by an additional sum of over seven and three-quarter million dollars which was found to be essential for the purpose of taking care of the commitments made by the government, including governor general's warrants which amounted to nearly $200,000.
I submit that this expenditure is entirely beyond what should be expended by this country at this time, and I find my vindication for the observations I am about to make in the statement made to this house over a quarter of a century ago by Right Hon. W. S. Fielding, the then Minister of Finance. Meeting a motion deprecating large expenditures and swollen budgets, the then Minister of Finance used these words:
Let me say that so far as my hon. friend's object was to utter a word of warning as to the need of moderation in our expenditure, as to the need of looking to the future, I entirely sympathize with him and welcome that word, no matter from what quarter it may come. There is always a tendency, whether in personal or in national affairs, for men in times of great prosperity to forget the future, and it is always well that some cool head should be found to call attention to the conditions of the day, to the possible change of these conditions, and to the necessity of adapting our policy not only to things as they are, but to things as they may be at no distant day. I am always glad to find any one calling attention to that phase of our public affairs. So strongly impressed have I been with the necessity of at all times keeping that in mind, that in the various statements which it has been my privilege to present in the form of budget speeches, at the moment when we attained the greatest prosperity, I had deemed it well to call attention to the serious view which my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) presented to-day, and which I have presented from time to time, as to the necessity of looking to the future.
Now, sir, on more than one occasion during the progress of this session I have ventured to point out to the house that the conditions existing at the present time indicate very clearly to those who read the commercial barometers and to those who are concerned about the future that we should exercise great prudence and foresight in connection with our expenditures. I have already directed attention to what was done during the year which ended on March 31, 1928, and it is only necessary to turn to the Canada

Public Expenditure-Mr. Bennett
Year Book and to look at the total expenditures of this country during the last few years to observe that while we are prosperous, in the sense that we are collecting large revenues, we are also making enormous expenditures, which it would have been thought impossible for this country to make a few years ago. If any hon. member will refer to the Canada Year Book for 1928 he will find the total expenditures indicated at page 765, and it will be seen that in the last year before the war, the year ending March 31, 1914, the total expenditures of this country for all purposes were $186,241,048. By the year 1926 these figures had risen, in that short period of only twelve years, to $355,186,423. Included in the latter figure were sums of money advanced to the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Government Merchant Marine but it will be observed that hi previous years the sums expended for these services were larger than in the year 1926. Therefore we have the conditions to which I have referred,- namely enormously increasing expenditures, increasing it seems to me beyond all possible opportunity for us to overtake them by any revenues we may possibly hope to collect, if we are to bring about that reduction of taxation which is so essential to the development of our industrial life. If a citizen of this country had been told ten or fifteen years ago that the Dominion of Canada, with its population so little increased in that period of time as the figures indicate, would increase its expenditure by almost 100 per cent, he would have thought it impossible that it could be so, yet there are the figures before us.
When we turn to the revenue statements at page 761 we find that the total consolidated revenues of this country were as follows :
1922		 $382,271,571
1923		 403,094,210
1924		 406,582,840
1925		 351,515,392
1926		 382,893,009
At pages 3037 and 3038 of the Canada Gazette for this year we find that our revenues for the year ending March 31, 1927, amounted to $385,668,925.31, and that for the year ending March 31, 1928, they rose to the largest sum we have on record in this country, namely, $417,127,500, in round figures. Our expenditures for 1927 amounted to $324,239,424.97, including $10,000,060' for the Canadian National Railways and $426,817.14 for the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. For the year ending March 31, 1928, the last fiscal year, our expenditures amounted to $329,966,715.67, including a million dollars for the Canadian 
Government Merchant Marine, or in other words an increase of $5,727,290.70 over the preceding year.
Under present conditions, Mr. Speaker, is there anything to warrant the enormous increase of over five and three-quarter million dollars in the expenditures of this country in 1928, over 1927, when the expenditures during that year had reached the enormous figure to which I 'have referred? Any expenditure of this country in excess of $325,000,000 is an enormous expenditure for the Dominion of Canada with its limited population. If this government were more anxious about the practice of economy, about seeing that one hundred cents of value is given for every dollar of expenditure, the conditions would be mudh better than they are now. What Mr. Fielding said twenty-five years ago is more than true to-day. We are getting into the habit of dealing with thousands and millions of dollars as though they were a mere bagatelle, and we think that for some reason we may make these vast expenditures without any regard whatever to the future. I think the time has come when we should take stock of the situation. I know how pleasant it is for governments to spend money. Their supporters demand that they shall spend money; the Minister of Public Works is besieged by applications for public buildings, and every department of the public service is asked for money. And yet this was the condition which prevailed in the United States when President Coolidge took charge, when he appointed General Lord and his successors to the position of director of budgets, and brought about a saving, as has been pointed out by me, of over one million dollars a day in interest charges alone. In his message to congress he referred to the debt of the country as being the greatest economic menace that threatened the life of the United States. I have directed attention to it already, and bearing in mind the vast expenditures to which this country committed itself in 1927, for the year ending 31st March, 1928, I again direct the attention -of my fellow members to the language of Mr. Fielding. You may possibly say to me, "But what are the particulars; what are the details? Why is it that you say these expenditures may not give an adequate return to the people of this country?" I refer the house to the language used by the then leader of the opposition, Mr. Borden; and I might mention that in his view he was supported by an eminent English statesman whose utterance I shall not delay to read. Mr. Borden said:
Now, where an opposition are not able to get, within a reasonable time, and without

Public Expenditure-Mr. Bennett
unduly protracting the session, information which would enable them to discriminate between hundreds of items brought down to this house, when they are unable to get information which would put them in the same position for forming an opinion that the government are in, the proper duty for an opposition is to protest against excessive expenditure, to throw upon the government the responsibility of making it, knowing as they do that the government have within their power the means of reducing that expenditure by eliminating from it items which are less worthy of public appropriation than those W'hieh are necessary to be made. That is the view which has been put forward in the English House of Commons as a sound principle, that an opposition in protesting, as we have protested, against undue expenditure, have discharged their duty without dealing in detail vuth the particular items of the expenditure brought down by the government.
Let us then, in the light of that statement and the observations which I have just made, look at the expenditures to which we are committed for the years 1928-29, in other words the fiscal year ending the 31st March, 1929. I wonder if this house has considered what money we have voted; I wonder if the Minister of Finance has taken due cognizance of the extent to which we have made commitments for the future. Let me read them to this house. The main estimates for this year committed us to an expenditure of 5373,796,856.24. The first supplementary estimates committed us to a further expenditure of $10,583,611.91, and the further supplementary estimates committed this country to the expenditure of $1,000,200. Then let us look at the other sums to which we are committed. First there are the railways-well, I will not take them first-
But they are coming?

They are coming, yes.
The hon. gentleman seems to think it is a matter of very little importance, and yet I think, when he calmly considers the situation, he will realize what it means not only to himself but to his family, to place these increasing burdens upon the people of this country. The three items which I have mentioned make a total of $385,380,668.15.
But we did not stop there. We voted $3,000,000 to the Federal District Commission for the improvement of Ottawa, by Bill 218. We voted a $200,000 annuity by Bill 218 to the same authority. We voted an annuity of $75,000 to the National Battlefields Commission by Bill 34. We voted $200,000 per year for two years for level crossings by Bill 220. These items make a total of $388,855,668.15.
But we did not stop there. What further sums has this house committed this country
to? At the initiation of the government and at their request, we have voted $8,500,000 to the harbour of Quebec. It is admitted that the money is a direct charge upon this country and that it will not be repaid by the harbour itself; that was admitted by the hon. gentlemen w'ho assumed responsibility for that expenditure. We have voted $5,000,000 to the harbour of St. John, and $500,000 to the harbour of Halifax. These items total $14,000,000. It is perfectly true that all these items will not be expended this year, but it is also equally true that the money must be found some time by the taxpayers of Canada, at least in respect to the item of the Quebec harbour. We have committed this country to those expenditures, whether the money be paid to-day or to-morrow or next year or the year after.
But did we stop there? We did not; we went further. Last night we were voting, and to-day we will be called upon to vote-the government has the requisite majority behind it to vote it -$47,156,644.50 for the Canadian National Railways and for the Canadian Government Merchant Marine.
Does this house realize just what these stupendous figures mean in the way of taxation? But in addition to these sums, we also voted $3,500,000 for the terminal at Toronto, and voted a further sum, in excess of $22,689,575, in connection with the Canadian Northern Income Charge Act. These bonds were originally an obligation of the Canadian Northern railway, but they have become an obligation of this country because we know these companies cannot be allowed to go into liquidation or into the hands of a receiver because of our investment in them during the past ten years.

What is that total
again?

It is $22,689,575, under
Bill No. 153. We have the stupendous total of nearly $450,000,000 outside of that obligation in connection with the income securities of the old Canadian Northern. I wonder if this house realizes that we are now faced with a budget of nearly half a billion dollars with less than ten millions of people who are already staggering under the burden of a debt of two and a half billions of dollars? In these buoyant days it is easy to talk in millions of dollars and find the money to meet these appropriations. We have not had the op- . portunity, as Mr. Borden pointed out when leader of the opposition, of considering the items in detail.

Take the votes, for instance, concerning expenditures west of the great lakes. How many of us have been afforded the opportunity to read all the necessary papers, documents and reports on these subjects, to discover whether these undertakings will serve any useful public purpose? Take the vast expenditures for civil government; take the expenditure, as shown by the return brought down to this house, in connection with the fleet of government automobiles in this city; take that alone. You say, "Oh, that is a piffling thing," but there it is. It runs into thousands and thousands of dollars increasing as the days go by, and yet no one seems to care. The other day I heard a gentleman who, it is true, is only an observer, a man who has lived in the capital a long time and who is not interested in politics, say that he had never before seen such reckless expenditures of public money in this country. If you walk down yonder, you will see a vacant piece of land which the Minister of Public Works has bought for a large sum of money to put a pavement on which will cost nearly three-quarters of a million dollars before it is finished. Land and buildings have been purchased just to secure a small area of land in the centre of the city. We look at the wreck of an old hotel and there is an expenditure of three millions of dollars with the commitments for the adjoining areas. We have a sum of $950,000 in two annuities alone in respect to the national battlefields and the improvement commission of this city, and to this there is added an annuity in connection with level crossings, making a total of $1,150,000.
Take the railway expenditures. What member of this house has any adequate appreciation of the railway figures? We sit here and laughingly vote $47,000,000 and we are voting by these supply bills nearly $100,000,000 more than the national debt of this country was before the war began. That is only fourteen years ago. Think of the commitments that have been brought about in that time. In England, France, continental Europe, the United States, with all their riches, they have approached these problems as men who are intent upon bringing about a shrinkage in expenditure and it is no answer for the Minister of Finance to say that every member who sits on this side of the house has been anxious to have additional sums spent in his constituency. Why would he not be when he sees the government recklessly throwing money away in every direction? Has one particular community to be singled out for

expenditure and the other left alone? The reason why hon. members on this side rise and ask that their constituencies be protected is that there are public buildings falling into decay, public works that are not being maintained, because, forsooth, the patronage evil is abroad in this country and the exchequer of Canada is being used to advance the political fortunes of the supporters of the administration. That is the real reason. There is no thoughtful man who travels by automobile throughout this country; there is no man who goes on our highways and observes the expenditures for post offices, wharves, docks, dredging in counties and districts that are returning supporters of the administration and then notes the lack of them in other communities. but realizes that if there is no necessity for them in the latter, there certainly is no excuse for them in the former. If, in other words, the public necessity does not demand that money should be expended for public* works in the sense I have indicated in constituencies that do not return supporters of the administration, that in itself is an indication that there is no public necessity for these expenditures in the other communities to which I have referred. That is patronage to the eyes of the most superficial observer.	_	_
I am not unmindful of the fact that it is easy to brush these things aside; that it is easy to say that this country is entering upon an era of unexampled prosperity and that there will be more revenues than ever before we have heard of available for our purposes. One of the premiers of the provinces within the last forty-eight hours, dealing with his experience in Canada under our profitless prosperity, said: "Your remedy is to obtain reduced taxation from the federal authorities." This country is groaning under the burden of present taxation. There are few more highly taxed countries than we are with such a vast area and such a small population.

I am not charged with
responsibility.
Oh, oh.

Once more it is the old
story of my very courteous and, in some particulars, easy-minded friend, the Minister of Finance, who asks: "What do you think about it?" When I have responsibility, I will tell him what I think about it. That is the reason this motion is before the house. It is because the government seems to shirk responsibility by asking somebody else what they think about the matter. It is easy to look at bank returns, at the returns of industry under profitless prosperity; it is easy to look at your statistics; but a Minister of Finance who would assume responsibility in this country for bringing about a policy of real economy, would be regarded with the greatest possible affection by the people. This might not make for popularity for the moment, but it would bring about that enduring admiration for his achievements in promoting thrift and economy which are the bases of all prosperity in the country.
Listen to what we heard this morning. The Minister of Finance this morning rose in his place and talked about the difficulties in connection with a slight expenditure for printing a few pamphlets to distribute over the country. There is more money spent here in a single month for automobiles for those who should not have them than would pay for the whole of this expenditure. If you look at the return that was brought down, it is calculated to make any Canadian blush with shame to see the expenditures made in connection with automobiles in this capital city of Ottawa. That is the minister's conception of economy. He is not going to print 25,000 copies of a report on the protein content of wheat. Why, he says, we must be economical; we must see how we are going to save our money, and then we are voting $39,000,000 for the national railways and duplicate hotel facilities at Halifax with an estimated loss, according to their own manager, of $100,000 per annum on one hotel. That is the government's idea of economy-lose $100,000 a year, but be economical in the matter of printing a few hundred pamphlets.
Look at the returns that have been brought down during the last few months; study them, and you will be convinced that no business man could for a single month maintain his business if the conditions indicated in those returns were allowed to continue. That is the position with respect to the matter. Is this a business administration or just a taxcollecting administration, gathering in the money for the purpose of disbursing it amongst its supporters? That is the question. Is this a business administration or not? I put the question to the committee last evening; I pointed out as carefully as I could-and I have not yet finished with respect to that- what is involved in regard to the expenditure in connection with the hotel at Halifax.
Oh, oh.

I have not, not by any means. I am pointing out what that involves. It involves a loss, as admitted by the technical adviser to this country's railway, of $100,000 a year with respect to one hotel, and now the minister says: Give us $1,250,000 and we will build another to duplicate the one already in existence. The government has either gone mad with extravagance or else is drunik with power and is without any sense ol responsibility. The administration thinks there will be no end as long as it can spend the money. Study the budgets in England and look at the economies they have effected; or if you are not governed by British precedent, go down to Washington and you will find that with all their wealth they would not think for a single moment of spending money in the manner in which we do. I have a considerable number of columns of figures that I might read to the house to show exactly what is going on in connection with various matters mentioned, but I will content myself with merely making this motion, because I cannot at this stage of the session take longer time in which to direct attention to the details. But I follow the time-honoured custom mentioned by Sir Robert Borden as the precedent for British statesmen in opposition dealing with matters of this kind, to protest against these swollen budgets, protest against these unnecessary expenditures, to protest in the name of the people who will have in the end to carry the burden and pay the taxes.
It is all right to rejoice in these days of seeming prosperity and say we have ample moneys and let us spend them. But there comes a day of reckoning, and that day you can almost see in the distance now. The trade returns of this country for the last month for which we have the figures show that our imports are, I believe, higher than they had been in any corresponding month in our history, and our exports had fallen to the lowest figure for years. There was an adverse balance of trade against us of $20,000,000 in round figures. That merely indicates that under the existing conditions created by the government opposite you have in Canada,
4044	COMMONS
Public Expenditure-Mr. Bennett
what? You have the possibility, nay, more than that, you have issued an invitation to the great mass producing industries to the south of us, now that there has been some slackening in their activities, to maintain full production in order that their overhead may be' taken care of, and their surplus products sent at cheap prices to the Dominion. We imported in April, 1928, more, I think, than we ever did in. any corresponding month in our history, $78,000,000, and our exports dwindled to $58,000,000. Is not that a warning to the minister?
Let him consult the financial heads of great institutions to the south of us. It is true that we have a vast, untouched estate, and that new wealth may be produced much more readily from that than from an old and cultivated estate. But it is also true that where we cultivate, it is necessary that we should sell, and if we find a curtailment and shrinkage of trade among the nations of the world, we find a limitation placed upon our ability to dispose of that which we produce. The minister knows that. He (has been, told time and time again by the great heads of financial institutions to be cautious, to look ahead. Every thoughtful business man is doing it; everybody is shortening sail except the' speculators. Do you realize, sir, that this great speculative era that we now have on the American continent is one fraught with possibilities of the gravest disaster for this country? The brokers' loans alone in New York last week were over $5,000,000,000, an unheard of figure. In this country speculation is rampant. Some people imagine that trading in pieces of paper upon which there are engraved words and figures constitutes the creation of new wealth. It is not so. The new wealth of the country is being created by the application of labour and capital to the natural resources of the country, and this trading in stock certificates, this great era of speculation in this country and on this continent, is one fraught with possibilities of the gravest danger to Canada, because we have not as they have in the United States a vast accumulation of wealth that will enable us to meet the approaching conditions with ease.
Look at the movement of securities; look at the movement of gold; look at every indication there is with respect to speculation in this country. I know great brokers' houses that have declined to take new accounts in this country for over twelve months, one perhaps the greatest brokerage house in this country, because they fear what they see in the distance. But no one in the government seems to care, and if we point out the con-

ditions we are " pessimists ", if we venture to direct attention to the conditions we are " decrying our country ". That is the talk that hon. gentlemen opposite hurl at us and before the country. But I recall the language of one who was regarded in after years as one of the very greatest of British statesmen, who observed that when their orgy was through, when they had at last recovered from the debauch in which they were then enjoying themselves, possibly then in their sober and quiet moments they would look back and recall the warning that had been given by those who, looking into the future as best they could, guided by those economic signs that were apparent, and by beacon lights, warning of the future, had pointed out the conditions as they also had come to pass. You perhaps will look back upon our warnings, and perhaps remember with at least some degree of fair-minded justice the observations that were made by those of us who have pointed out the national disaster that is inevitable if this orgy of mad expenditure continues.
It is for these reasons, sir, that we make this motion, hoping and believing that at least it will have the effect of directing the attention of the administration to the seriousness of the condition that is involved in the vast expenditures of public moneys that must be raised by the taxpayers, that is by the people of Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) closed his very interesting speech by giving us as a reason for the introduction of this amendment that he wanted to advise the government to go slowly in the expenditure of public funds. It occurred to me 'as I listened to my hon. friend's speech, that it was more of a lesson to his own followers that he was presenting because I have in mind that in recent weeks we on this side of the house have been attacked, not because we were spending too much money, but' because we were not spending money enough in certain parts of the country.
I find no fault with the amendment introduced by my hon. friend. It is a part of party etiquette that at some time just before prorogation the leader of the opposition should attempt to present a resolution broad enough to allow everyone to come in under it and 'vote for it, and so to-day he has presented 'what might properly be termed a blanket [DOT]resolution.
My hon. friend, like myself, is an admirer of that great finance minister of Canada, the Right Hon. Mr. Fielding. He has quoted

Public Expenditure-Mr. Robb
Mr. Fielding frequently this morning. There was one observation that Mr. Fielding generally made in answer to all such speeches that my hon. friend did not quote. I recall it very well, as will my hon. friend and all of those who sat in the house with Mr. Fielding. Mr. Fielding used to say that every person was in favour of economy for the other fellow, but no one wanted economy applied to his own particular constituency.
After all, Mr. Speaker, I am not finding any fault with the statement that my hon. friend has made regarding the wisdom of Canada going slow in the matter, for instance, of speculation, and in Canada going slow in expenditure, but there is a reasonable attitude to take. There was a time in the history of Canada when it was very necessary to go slow and to economize, but as the country grows and progresses, the government that does not take care of the growing needs of the country is falling down in its duty. It seems to me that the real test as to how wisely the finances of a country are being administered is to make a comparison of the expenditures with the revenue; to ascertain the taxes that are imposed upon the people, and then to determine whether the government, in carrying on the affairs of the country, have been doing so economically, and in such a way as gradually to reduce the burden of taxation bearing so heavily upon the people.
I welcome the opportunity of a comparison of this government's administration with the administration of our predecessors, but before proceeding may I point out that all these statements that we sometimes hear and sometimes read of the government-or rather parliament, because it is an attack on all parties- railroading through three hundred million dollars odd of estimates, contain a good deal of rubbish. Parliament has already authorized a substantial part of these estimates-they are statutory. For instance, if hon. gentlemen will look at the summary on pages 4 and 5 of the estimates they will find the amounts authorized by statute. The statutory estimates this year amount to about $150,608,000. Civil government estimates total $12,363,000. These civil government estimates are the result of the Civil Service Commission appointed by parliament, and parliament guards very jealously any encroachment on the rights of that commission. It is the Civil Service Commission that increases or decreases the salaries of civil servants throughout the country. Then there are the war pensions. Those already authorized by parliament total some $39,000,000 odd. In other words, sir,
parliament is called upon closely to scrutinize about one hundred million dollars of government estimates; the balance had already been scrutinized by parliament, and parliament itself had authorized the expenditure.
I said a moment ago that the real test of administration was a comparison as between revenues and expenditures and reduction of taxes under Liberal and Tory governments. At this late hour I have no desire to delay the house. I know hon. gentlemen are all anxious to proceed with the business yet remaining to be dealt with. But may I just briefly put on record a comparison of the revenues and expenditures under this government and under our immediate predecessors? For the fiscal year ending March 31, 1921, the total estimates were $535,790,643. For the fiscal year ending March 31, 1922-the Conservatives were in power for nine months, but they were wholly responsible for the estimates which were prepared in the previous year-the estimate? were $446,747,947. And what were the receipts in 1921 when the total estimates were over $535,000,000? In that year the total receipts were $436,292,184. In the following year when the estimated expenditure was over $446,000,000, the total receipts were $382,271,571. Those years showed a deficit and an increase of taxes. The duty of this government on its coming into office and resuming responsibility for carrying on the affairs of the country was to pay off the debts of our predecessors. We have succeeded in doing that, and at the same time materially reducing taxation.
Now, what sort of balance sheet did these hon. gentlemen show when they were in office. I welcome this change of heart on the part of the Conservative party as demonstrated this morning by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition. But our Tory friends in opposition are always strong for economy. When they are charged with the responsibilities of office I recall the famous words, to be found in Hansard, of a distinguished representative from one of the maritime provinces, who, after this party had been in office for some fifteen years and had accumulated surpluses, and wa3 succeeded by the Tory party, said one afternoon when the estimates were under discussion-my colleagues the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice will remember his words:
Why economize? Let us speed away and spend the money.
That is the attitude.

Dash away.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That was the attitude of
the Conservative party when entrusted with responsibility in 1912. What was the change in the debt position of the country during the administration of the Tory party? According to the public accounts they increased the national debt in 1920 by $674,337,591; in 1921 by $92,010,359; in 1922 by $81,256,818. In the first year of our administration the national debt was increased by $31,641,067. But let us keep in mind that we had inherited some contracts that had been given out by our predecessors and we had to provide for them. What has been the record of the departmental finances since that day? In 1924 the reduction of debt was $35,993,593; in 1925, $345,589; in 1926 $27,706,586; in 1927, $41,896,729; and for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1928, when the books were closed the reduction of debt was $51,125,436. And notwithstanding that, we have been able to reduce the taxes bearing so heavily upon the people.
Under these conditions with growing surpluses, with the reduction in taxation, it is perhaps very natural that throughout Canada there should be increased demands for expenditure. I recall, about a year ago I think, one of the biggest of the big financial men of this country, himself a strong advocate of economy-he had been preaching it for some time-saying to me: "I am afraid, Mr. Robb, that Mr. Ring s government may be carrying this economy a little too far; this country is growing, and you must provide for the carrying on of the affairs of Canada in a reasonable way." I suppose he voiced public opinion fairly well. At least he voiced the opinion that we have heard in this chamber during this session. I am wondering who is going to vote for this blanket resolution for economy. Who is going to vote against these estimates that we are presenting to-day? Are the hon. members who come from the great city of Toronto going to vote against these expenditures, and for greater economy? Are hon. members from Hamilton going to vote for a reduction in the estimates? No cities in Canada have received more by direct votes than these two cities in Ontario. No person will say that they are ardent supporters of the government; but the growing demands of those cities did require some additional expenditure. And my hon. friends from the maritime provinces, are they going to vote for this blanket resolution for economy? If so, 
they are going to vote against all the speeches they have made within the last month. They held up this house for the better part of two days telling us that we had not been providing sufficient expenditure to carry on the affairs of the country. But it is not the province of Ontario and the maritimes alone who have been asking for increased expenditures. My hon. friends down in yonder group have been chiding the government because, forsooth, we have not been spending money enough in their part of the country. I have under my hand a statement showing that just one day, when my colleague the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Elliott) was presenting his estimates, seventeen gentlemen opposite rose each in his place and demanded an increased expenditure in his own county. We were chided because we were not providing for public buildings or wharves or something in the counties those hon. gentlemen have the honour to represent. A few days later my colleague was again before the committee, and again there were demands for increased expenditure. It is possible there were some demands from this side, but it so happens that on the list I have in my hand there are seven names of hon. gentlemen, one from the city of Quebec, but all the others, gentlemen now facing me, very genial chaps. And would you believe it, among those asking for increased expenditures was my hon. friend who has presented the resolution this morning.

That is hardly a correct statement. What I pointed out was that the city of Calgary, with its large revenues, was without a public building although other places had public buildings, because they had returned government supporters 'and Calgary had not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend pointed out
that Calgary was entitled to a public building and he was on sound ground. He was no worse than other members in that respect. I was in Calgary last fall and I am bound to say I think my hon. friend was right. But surely he cannot chide us for having increased expenditures when he and his friends are finding fault because we have not been spending money enough.
I have no desire to delay the house longer. The policy of this government is to live within our means; to provide annually surpluses instead of deficits; to reduce annually the taxes bearing so heavily upon the people. Our record is good in that regard and we have succeeded in reducing the public debt. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that so long as a country is able to present in its an-

Public Expenditure-Mr. Irvine
nual statements a surplus of revenue over expenditures, a reduction in the national debt .and a reduction in taxation, blanket resolutions such as this, coming from hon. gentlemen opposite who individually are urging the government to spend more money in their own constituencies, are not very weighty. My hon. friend is making a brave attempt to rally his friends around him to get them to vote on a resolution which might possibly send the government to prorogation with a little less majority than we have been having recently. But back in the country gentlemeu who vote against these expenditures will be met by their constituents with this comment: "Well, you will have to do some explaining as to why you are voting against a government that is providing generously for carrying on public works within our different counties."

On a question of privilege, may I mention one matter? The Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) has sent me a slip indicating that under Bill 204, which increases to $10,500,000, the amount of security that might be issued in connection with the Toronto terminals, $7,000,000 had already been issued and the new amount would be only $3,500,000. The act calls for $10,500,000 but $7,000,000 has already been issued and the additional amount, as I have stated, is only $3,500,000. I thank the hon. gentleman. I had not the information as to the exact amount.

I desire to make an observation or two on the motion which has been presented by the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). It is of course not an opportune time to attempt to analyse the entire budget of the nation, especially when there is such anxiety evinced on all sides of the house for a speedy closing of the session-an anxiety which I share. I think I might say at the outset that there are very grave charges indeed involved in the leader of the opposition's resolution, charges which perhaps merit a great deal more attention than we shall be able to give them at the present time. It is true the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) has characterized the motion as being a part of party etiquette, and in that regard the charges, judging by the past at least are well founded. Then the minister replies in party etiquette style also by pointing out to us that this is not the only government whch has made large expenditures. That too I regard as party etiquette. I want to point out that I was one who urged
the government for larger expenditures at a time when Canada was passing through a very difficult period of depression. At that time I found that the house generally had caught the gloom, and everywhere was insisting that the government should restrict its expenditures and thus further force the country into depression. Following the same policy I would say that this is the time when Canada should restrict her expenditures as far as possible and start no new exploits which could be postponed for a few years, knowing that the depression will return. I do not wish to charge the government with not having followed that policy, for that policy has never been followed, and it cannot be followed until there is a sounder view perhaps of the expenditure of money in relation to the general prosperity of the country. There may be extravagance in many of the items which have passed the house; there may be extravagance in any one or other of the departments; and to that extent no doubt the charge of the leader of the opposition may be very well taken. On the other hand we are not in a position to know just whether there have been extravagances or not. For several years we have pressed from this section of the assembly that there ought to be a better method of examining the expenditures of the country. We have asked from time to time that estimates be either allocated to various standing committees of the house, or that special committees be appointed to attend to this matter. So far we have not received much encouragement. I do not know whether the present way of dealing with the estimates is also party etiquette and affords an opportunity for partisanship in this house. If that is so, it does not apply to this particular government but to all governments.
But I do insist that the government give us now some assurance that at subsequent sessions an attempt will be made to deal a little more efficiently with the examination of the expenditures of the country. Sitting here in committee of the whole, with party etiquette reigning on each side, wasting time asking foolish questions, putting the minister into a corner where he cannot answer and has not the information-all this is absolutely absurd, and for an intelligent assembly like this to proceed in that manner to vote the expenditure of approximately $500,000,000 is something I cannot understand.
While I am not supposed to be a business man, I assure you, Mr. Speaker, I would not proceed in that way. I think there are better

Public Expenditure-Mr. Mackenzie King
ways to do it, and if the Prime Minister is going to have anything to say on the amendment I hope he will give us some assurance that this question will be looked into and that in the future the estimates will be more carefully examined.
I agree to this extent with the Minister of Finance, that the amendment of the leader of the opposition is a blanket charge. There are many expenditures which we all agree must go on, and of course there may be some which should not be made. However, I say we have not the means of getting accurate information with respect to these matters. Of course I realize that perhaps the leader of the opposition could not do otherwise at this time than make a blanket charge, but in respect to the other point which the Minister of Finance brought out, when he asked who was going to vote against this amendment, I could tell him of people who might very well vote for it. I refer to the people of the western provinces, because when you look over the expenditures of the country you find that a very small percentage of them has been made there. So I think we could surely justify ourselves if we decided to support the amendment of the leader of the opposition. I do not know the exact percentage of the total expenditure which will be made in the western provinces, but I do know -that in other years less than 10 per cent went to those four western provinces, and I do not know that that percentage has been increased. I also know that in the west there is a growing feeling that in the eastern provinces large expenditures are made which are regarded by the man in the street as being for party purposes. I do not say that that is true; we do not know whether or not it is true because we have not had the opportunity to investigate. However, I will say that I have made no request to the government for the expenditure of money in my constituency. I did have an idea that we should have a new post office in the large, flourishing city of Bentley; I once thought I might ask for $5,000,000 or so to dredge out a harbour below my house on Blindman river, but not being persona grata I thought I had better not present those requests.
I will conclude, Mr. Speaker, by saying that in a growing country such as Canada our expenditures necessarily must grow with our increasing obligations. If we merely make a blanket charge that too much money has been spent I do not know that I could conscientiously support that view unless I had the information which, as I have indicated, we do not have. I hope that in the future we

will make larger expenditures, providing that they are made for the welfare of the nation and to meet the needs of the public service. I do not believe the people will be averse to the expenditure of the present budget, provided they are assured that the expenditure is made in a proper way. That is all I desire to say at this time.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) has just spoken with regard to the advisability of adopting a different method of considering the estimates. In particular he has suggested that the estimates should be submitted, as I understand it, either to a special committee for the purpose of considering all the estimates of the departments, or by departments to standing committees of the house which have to do with the different subjects to which -the estimates relate. 'May I say to my hon. friend that his suggestion is -one which the government had under consideration at the opening of this session. My hon. friend the leader of -the opposition (Mr. Bennett) will recall that at the beginning of the session I discussed with him the advisability of the different parties in the house adopting some more effective method of scrutinizing the supply requested by the government, some method which would enable members to hear what the officials of the departments had t-o say with respect to the several items included in the estimates. I entirely agree with my hon. friend that the system at present in force, under which a minister of the crown is necessarily dependent in the House of Commons on his deputy for much of the needed information with the deputy, also of necessity, often not wholly familiar with all the details of particular branches, is most unsatisfactory. Speaking for the government I would say that we would welcome a change in the present method, a change which would not only afford fuller opportunity for discussion but which would carry with it an obligation on the part of the heads of different branches of the public service to appear before a committee of the house and explain fully the reasons which have occasioned the recommendations which find their place in the estimates submitted to the house.
Having said this I would like to supplement my remarks further by saying that if we are not voted out of office as a result of this blanket amendment and if when another session comes around we still retain the confidence of the House of Commons, one of the first matters to which we will ask the house

Public, Expenditure-Mr. Evans
to give its attention and consideration will be the one mentioned by my hon. friend, namely that of arranging some method by which the estimates may to a greater or less extent be considered by a special committee or by the standing committees of the house.

If this amendment comes to a vote we will be placed in one of those awkward situations which come about as a result of the party system of government. We have been placed in this position more than once before, and the house need not be surprised at the way any hon. member of this small group may vote in connection with this amendment. We are now asked to decide between the tremendous expenditures and some of the votes which are made for party purposes only. Not long ago an amendment was debated on this side of the house condemning the government for not implementing the Duncan report 100 per cent. That whole report is the result of a false fiscal system, and so long as special privilege is catered to in this country situations of that kind will develop in the future more rapidly than has been the case in the past.
To-day if we vote for the government we vote for millions and millions of utter waste this year in connection with the demolishing of splendid buildings in this city which were built for permanent use, without the construction of one highway in western Canada where the people cannot even go to market or get their mail for certain weeks in the year. Next year we must have some new method for consideration of our public expenditures.

['Let me continue with\nmy argument. Other employers pf labour have in some instances refused to take back striking employees. That is a perfectly understandable position to take, but when they did take them back they paid them at the current rate of wages. If, for instance, an iron master took back a mechanic, he paid him the wages that were payable to a mechanic. I have no hesitation in stating that at least ninety or ninety-five per cent of the membership of this House of Commons are in favour of an increase in the indemnity. I am myself in favour of it, not only on my own behalf but on behalf of large numbers of hon. members. I am not exactly one of the oldest members of the house, but I come pretty near to be one of the oldest members, and I consider that in justice and fairness to the members of this house, and in the interests of the country at large, it would only be fair and right that the indemnity should be increased, and if the thing is to be done, I do not see why it should not be done this year as well as at any other time.
In 1920 I had the honour of speaking in this house when the question of an increased indemnity, proposed by the Right Hon. Sir Robert Borden, came before us. The great majority of the members were in favour of that increase, which was concurred in by both political parties and by the house. At that time it was very clearly stated that the indemnity was not adequate remuneration for the sacrifices and expenses that had to be borne by the members who had to sit here in Ottawa for five or six and sometimes seven months in the year. The members of this House of Commons, representing the people, are supposed to make pecuniary sacrifices, and in some instances they can well afford to do so. We have in this house some of the wealthiest men in the country, who can well afford to give up their private business and devote their lives to the service of the country. But, on the other hand, we have representatives of the people in this house who belong to the farming class, men representative of labour, industrial representatives, and merchants, and for these classes it is well known that there is not much reward in politics. After a man has given years of service to his country, and his private business has been ruined, he is left at home, and sometimes his family has to suffer as well as himself for the sacrifices that he has made in political life. We have lost many valuable men who have had to leave the political arena and go into private business, or seek employment in the civil service or on the bench, simply because they could not afford to stay in politics. On both sides of the house at the present time there are many members who are looking for a judgeship or some other position for the reason that they cannot afford to remain in politics. I think, Mr. Speaker, that it is in the best interests of this country that this question should be brought before the house, and that the house

Only a few years ago I had quite an experience in that regard; I refused the drug to a young woman, with the consequence- that she ended her life in the river. to discover whether the applicants are suffering from conditions that would prevent their entering this country. That is done in the ordinary way. My hon. friend spoke to me yesterday in regard to this matter, in connection with a complaint that he had received from one of his constituents in regard to the exposure of a member of the family who had gone up for examination. I do not know why we should worry so much. These men are trained medical men; they are all graduates and have had experience, and I think we are all sufficiently familiar to-day with the work of the profession and the facilities that are used by the profession, to ascertain the conditions that exist in the individual who comes before them. If a physical examination is necessary, then the one to judge as to the extent of that examination is the examining officer. If an individual walks into his office with a good firm step, he can almost be sure that that individual has not flat feet or bunions or other deformity, and he would not worry about that; but if the individual hobbled in, the examining officer would probably want him to expose his extremities to see what defects were there. In the examination there should be, I think, an examination of the vital organs, such as the heart and lungs. That means a certain exposure of the chest if it is done properly. If the examining officer finds, as he proceeds that there is reason to believe that there is some deformity or unusual condition of the spine, he should examine the spine. If he thinks there is some condition involving the gall bladder or liver, that should be examined. I think we shall have to leave this matter entirely to the examining officer, and our only concern is to see that the examination takes place under proper conditions. If a female immigrant is going before the medical examining officer, and there is not a female medical officer, there should be a female attendant, and I think that is the practice. I do not think we should be very sensitive in regard to these matters, because in our everyday life we go to our own physician, and there is no question in regard to giving him the opportunity to make the proper examination.
They know him.

I desire to bring
to the attention of the Minister of Justice the criminal statistics of Canada. We have been led to believe that our penal institutions are
being flooded with foreigners, but in looking over the statistics I find that suggestion is absolutely unfounded. Taking the penitentiaries report, I notice these percentages. From 1917 to 1926 the percentage of Canadian-born in our penitentiaries was 63.4; in 1926, 66.6. The percentage of those from Great Britain and other British possessions occupying our penitentiaries was, from 1917 to 1926, 14 per cent; in 1926, 14.2 per cent; and of those from the United States, for the same periods, the percentages are 6.4 and 5.1 respectively. Taking the foreign-born in our penitentiaries, from 1917 to 1926, the percentage was 16.2; in 1926 1 4.1.	I am not going to take up
the percentages according to proportion of population, but I desire to direct the attention of the committee to the fact that the only percentage increase in the population of our penitentiaries occurs in our Canadian-born. As to education, we have for years been led to believe that the illiterate form the main percentage of our penitentiary inmates, but this is not borne out by the figures. Taking the illiterate criminals, in 1924 the percentage was 2.7, in 1925, 3.1 and in 1926, 2.8. Of the next class, the elementary, that is, those educated up to matriculation, the percentage was 81.7 in 1924, 78.4 in 1925 and 75 in 1926. Coming to the superior educated, that is, those who reached a higher stage, the percentage was only 1.2 in 1924, 1.2 in 1925 and .9 in 1926. Let me point out this: the illiterate were not increasing in percentage; the superior educated were not increasing but decreasing. Rather, the increases came from those who had gone through our public schools up to the threshold of higher education.
Then we come to juvenile delinquency. In 1925 the total was 8,739. Of these, 8,064 were boys and 675 girls. In 1926 the number was 8,846. Of these the boys numbered 8,245 and the girls 601. The total increase in the juvenile delinquents is 107; while there was a gross increase in boys of 181 there was a decrease in girls of 74.
Now to summarize. So far as the penitentiaries are concerned, I have a few points which I wish to direct to the attention of the minister. I will not touch the jails and asylums because the same considerations will apply to any increase there. First, the increase is coming from our own Canadian born; secondly, the increase is coming from the class who have received elementary education; thirdly, our juvenile delinquents are increasing. I think the time has come when the Justice department, in conjunction with our provinces, should take into consideration this serious

Supply-Justice
situation. It is very grave when you consider that the boys going through our schools -those boys who have not gone on to higher education-are increasing in delinquency, and the further fact that the boys are increasing in delinquency while the number of girls is decreasing. In my opinion the time has come, if we are to meet this situation at all, when the Justice department should enter upon some investigation of the cause for such a state of affairs. It is terrible when you think of the increase in delinquency amongst our boys. There must be some cause for it, and the Department of Justice and the departments of the attorneys general in the provinces should now take the matter up.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: What suggestion has my hon. friend to offer with regard to the method?

In the first place
I would advise the minister that the time has come when he should put his foot down upon the present practice of sending boys to the penitentiary. There is no use in saying that it is not going on; it is going on and the boys are there. There are to-day in the penitentiaries boys of fifteen, sixteen and seventeen.	I know the minister will tell
me that they are sent there by the police magistrates, and that this is a matter over which he has no control. These boys are placed side by side with life inmates of the penitentiary. That is something that the minister can control-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Quite so.

-iif he cannot control their admission. Then there is another situation. In Ontario we owe a great deal of the improvement in the province to the late Hon. W. J. Hanna. He provided an institution to which these boys might be sent. It worked well for a while but it is not working out at the present time. There is a little of the devil in these boys; there is no question about that. As soon as they escape from the institution they are taken and sent to the penitentiary. Ninety boys out of that institution, because they escaped, have been sent to the penitentiary.
There are two things which I want to impress upon the minister. First, the minister should have his officials, or the official in every institution, take up this matter with the younger people and find out just what was the beginning of their career. That he can do in the asylums and a few other places. He can then cooperate with the provinces, and that is something that can be done in the

prisons, jails and so forth. We ought to be able in that way, far better than by taking the matter up through clubs and other institutions, to ascertain the cause in every case. We can thereby discover whether it is due to the shows or to books, literature that has influenced them, or anything else. We should be able to find out in the majority of cases what started the boy in his course of crime. The second point is this: the time has come when there should be a more modern treatment of boy offenders than there is today. I do not agree that the Justice department or the attorney general's department in any province should ever let out of their hands the treatment of a boy after he has been delinquent. That is done now. There are private persons running schools and so forth, and I will mention one circumstance which will show how ridiculous the treament is. Two boys in my city were convicted. One never had a crime recorded against him and the other was a chronic offender. The police magistrate and the chief of police did not want them back in the city. These two boys were sent up; the one who was thoroughly under the influence of the chronic offender had never committed a crime. How did they treat these two boys? The boy who had never committed a crime was sent up there on the understanding that if he served a few months he would be sent home, but when he got to this school the Department of Justice and the department of the attorney general took the ground that they could not interfere because this was a privately run institution for the treatment of boys. They insisted that this boy who had never before been in trouble should be retained in that institution the same length of time as the chronic offender. Finally they are sent home and if that boy ever had a chance he did not have it then. He was thoroughly under the influence of the chronic offender.
This is a serious situation and in my opinion the Department of Justice and the departments of the attorneys general should cooperate with a view to solving the problem. If there is a cause it should be removed. I think I have demonstrated to-day that the foreign born element is not flooding our penitentiaries at least: the percentage there according to population is .02 in the case of the Canadian bom and .04 in the case of the foreign born. So that there is no flooding on the part of the foreign born. In the second place the increase in delinquency is coming from our own Canadian bom. Now we ought to be able to handle the situation and find a

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend from Kingston has
certainly called the attention of the committee to an important and serious condition and I may assure him that anything I can possibly do to decrease the number of offences among young people, or at least to check increases in crime, I shall be only too glad to do. Of course, as he says himself, these young people come under our department only after they have been convicted. We are not in contact with them in any way prior to their having been sentenced by the courts. However, I am quite willing to discuss this matter with the attorneys general of the various provinces and to cooperate with them to effect any reform which would remedy this condition of things.
I am glad my hon. friend has directed attention to the untruth of the statement so often made that the large proportion of inmates in the penitentiaries are foreign bom. I think wre may modestly confess that in this country we are breeding our own criminals, and we should not charge other countries with sending them here.
I am strongly in sympathy with my hon. friend in connection with the reform he suggests having to do with young offenders, and I have already stated in this house that I do not think it fair to put young people sixteen, seventeen or eighteen years of age in continuous contact with hard-boiled criminals. They are not given a chance to reform, and I thank my hon. friend for having spoken on this matter to-day. When the estimates are being prepared next year this will help me to convince my colleagues that the money will be well spent to provide for the construction of special institutions for young offenders. We should segregate those young people and give them a chance to reform. I do not know whether one institution would be sufficient; personally I think there should be two of them, one for eastern Canada and one for western Canada. This wall mean quite an expenditure of money, but I think we owe it to out young people that this money should be spent. So far as I am concerned I can assure my hon. friend that I am in sympathy with his suggestion and I will try to convince the government and parliament next year that money should be provided for this purpose.

I am sure we have all listened with interest to the remarks of the Minister of Justice, but some of us have listened to somewhat similar statements made year after year; we are told something is going to be done, yet years pass by and there is very little change indeed.
I hold in my hand the annual report of the superintendent of penitentiaries. For some years he has been asking the Minister of Justice to make certain changes; the Minister of Justice has assured us that he will try to persuade the government to make these changes and parliament to endorse the necessary expenditures, but I am quite sure that parliament is more than ready to make these changes now. I do not see why it should be such a tremendous task to persuade the government to carry out the recom-mendatioms of their own officials, especially when they are so reasonable and When they have been adopted in other places. Even on this busy day-and I do not think these things should be left to the last moment-I venture to take a few minutes to put on record these recommendations made by the superintendent. First he recommends the segregation and classification of young inmates; again he recommends the opening of a mental disease hospital. These reforms have been urged again and again by different societies throughout the country, and I do not see why they should be delayed for so long. The report also recommends the segregation of habitual criminals. I think that has been agitated for the past ten years, and I wonder how soon the government will take action?
Then it is recommended that more work be furnished to the inmates. Only last year the director of industry held a little exhibition in this very building in an attempt to persuade the members of this house to take some action which would induce the government to provide more work for the criminals. It is an astonishing thing that these officials who are close to the prisoners and who see their needs have to come almost on their knees to the higher officials begging that something be done, while the minister comes a.nd tells us in his turn that he is going to try to persuade the government to do something. Perhaps I am putting it rather strongly, but I should like to see action taken, as indeed t-he government have indicated that action will be taken. Unfortunately such assurances have been given in the past, but year after year we have to face this unsatisfactory state of affairs.
If we could not supply work to the individuals inside these various institutions; then there are roads to be built and ther*'

is land clearing work to be done. I was through one of our penal institutions in western Canada last year and saw the need for work of this kind. I wonder why we could not employ some of these men to build some of the roads which are so much needed; I am sure they would be much better off out in the open air under proper supervision than they would be cooped up in their cells. You may say that is not sufficient punishment, but I think it is helpful treatment if they are under proper supervision and are required to work for the state instead of working for their own personal advantage.
Then there is the further question of the payment of prisoners for their work. Some years ago the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) after working for two years, suceeded in having a resolution passed by this house approving of the payment of prisoners. I had rather imagined that a resolution passed by this house after full discussion was almost equivalent to legislation, and certainly that it formed a mandate for the government upon which they might be expected to act. That resolution was adopted two or three years ago, yet prisoners are not being paid any worth-While sum, and their families are still being supported by the municipalities in which they live. Very often the families are punished more than the prisoners themselves.
I do not want to read the Whole list of recommendations; I think we are all convinced of the need for these changes, and I am sure the country would welcome the adoption of these recommendations.

And further on, clause 26:
The mere provision of work is not, in the opinion of the committee, sufficient.
