And again:
If anything but evil is to follow from punishment by imprisonment for long terms, it is, in the opinion of the committee, essential that such provision should be made as will allow the convict to earn at least something toward the support of his dependents during his confinement or of himself after his release.
With that I think the Minister of Justice agrees in principle, and I believe the government and the members of the house agree also. As the minister said, they agreed back in 1926 to the resolution moved by the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) which was carried successfully and1 I think without a dissenting voice.
Turning to the statutes of this country, I find in the act respecting penitentiaries, subclause 3 of clause 62, the following:
The convicts may be employed in labour under the control of the crown.
I have no hesitation in stating that considerably more labour could be diverted to the penitentiaries in this country by the government than is being done to-day. If the government is in earnest about this matter there is no need to draw the herring of the labour organizations across the trail. Later on the time may come when there will be an excuse for it, but as long as the government is going outside the penitentiaries for work that can be done just as efficiently within, work done in an excellent way and under excellent supervision, then I submit the Minister of Justice has not made out a case for delay. I most earnestly urge that the recommendations of the superintendent, Mr. Hughes, and the recommendations of this house dating away back to 1921, be carried out without further delay. There are cases of hardship and cruelty arising out of the non-action of the government in this matter.
In my own particular riding I have a case of a man committed to gaol. He probably deserved to go there, but he left a wife and three children absolutely dependent upon

Supply-Justice

charity. They had almost to go round from door to door, and were forced to seek assistance from the municipality and board of trade. This man was a sort of transient prize fighter, and he could have been employed at most useful work. As a matter of fact I understand he became an excellent shoemaker while in prison, but received nothing for his work. He should have been paid and that money could have gone back to his dependents and relieved them of the stigma of having to look to charity for their existence. The wife and children were punished much more than the convict, and I most earnestly urge on the Minister of Justice and the Prime Minister that no further delay should be permitted in increasing the amount of crown work for penitentiaries.

While this vote is before the committee I would like to say a word regarding the Manitoba penitentiary, which is situated in my constituency. First of all I want to pay a tribute to the very capable and efficient manner in which this institution is being run. The warden and officials seem to realize their responsibilities and appreciate the fact that they are dealing with human beings, and appear to be doing their best for the unfortunate individuals who are under their care. I agree in large measure with the words of the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland). I visit this institution very often, and I have seen the men at their work. It seems to me that when a man is doing some constructive work, when he is creating something, he takes an interest in it and from that time on it is easier to make progress in reforming him.
A great deal of the work that is being done at this institution at the present time is in the nature of building. The inmates have constructed some very fine buildings in the last few years and they are a credit to the institution. But I should like to direct the attention of the Minister of Justice to the houses that the government own at that institution. They own in all some thirty houses which are not a credit to the government of Canada. They are old houses; they are a disgrace to the community and they disfigure the landscape. They are not modem in any way; they are without basements, and without furnaces. I suggest to the minister that when he goes west he look into this and see if he cannot agree with me that it would be advisable to have a nice group of cottages or bungalows, fully modem, that could be heated from the central steam heating plant of the institution.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We will visit it together.

Yes. These houses
could be rented to the guards and officials of the institution and interest on the money invested in them could be earned in that way. Without a great deal of outlay some houses could be constructed there that would be a credit to the department, which certainly cannot be said of the present buildings.
Another matter to which I wish to refer- and I have mentioned it in the house before- is that the f'arm in connection with that institution might well be run in connection with or under the supervision of the experimental farm as a demonstration farm. I am sorry to say that we have a great deal of labour in that institution which is well situated in every way to make an ideal demonstration farm for that district. All I would suggest now is that the work be supervised by the officials of the demonstration farm at Brandon, and in that way it would become an object lesson to the farmers in the district. At this late stage in the session I will not detain the house by saying any more on the matter, but I hope the minister will look into it when he goes west this summer.

I desire to ask the Postmaster General a few questions before I mention some facts that have been furnished to me. Will the minister tell the committee what air mail contracts have been let, and between what points?
I have the information here. Between Montreal and Rimouski, a distance of 330 miles, the contract price was $49,500.

Montreal to Father Point
is the same thing?

Yes; we go to Rimouski.
Between Montreal and Ottawa the Canadian
Transcontinental Airways, Limited, cover a distance of 110 miles and the contract price is $8,250; and between Montreal and Toronto, the Canadian Airways, Limited cover a distance of 330 miles, the contract price being $49,500.
Were tenders called for in all cases?

Tenders were called for on these routes and after they were received I called in the air board. There was such a diversity of tenders, between the lowest minimum and the highest, that it looked very much indeed as though persons were tendering who did not know what they were tendering on. As I say, I called in the air board of the National Defence department and I had a consultation that lasted two or three hours with the air board superintendent of this service, Mr. Coolican my deputy, and if I mistake not, the Minister of National Defence who was present for a while. We discussed the best methods to ascertain reasonable and proper prices for work of that description, and what machines should be employed to ensure safety and proper transportation. After this consultation we took the two companies who the year before last and last year had made trial flights between Rimouski and Montreal, and Montreal and Ottawa, and we arrived at the price which we submitted to the air board committee which takes all these matters into consideration. We decided upon a reasonable price which was $1.25 per mile, and on the basis of that $1.25 per mile we let the contract to these two companies who had been in our service previously.

Was that in accordance
with the lowest tender?
Yes.
Were there not tenders-

I am leading my hon.
friend astray. It was in accordance with the lowest tender, taking into consideration the proper class of machine to be used in this transportation business.
Were there not one or two other companies who tendered and whose total tender was lower than the one of the company to whom the contract was finally given at the price?
That is true.
And who were also reported on as good companies.

They may have been good companies, but the machines provided at the
Supply-Post Office

time were not such machines as we wished to use. One company-I forget the name- offered sixty cents a mile but it was not organized.
Mr. MAN-ION:	Which was that-the
Western Canadian? No, it would not-
It could not be that.

That is one of the older
companies. There is one other question. The minister mentioned different contracts between Montreal and Father Point and he mentioned one between Montreal and Toronto.
That is right.
Was there a contract between Montreal and Ottawa?

That is under negotiation.
We cannot definitely decide-although we are pretty close to the point of definite decision- until we have all arrangements concurred in between the Canadian and the American postal authorities. That contract will be called for within a very few days-in a short time, say a couple of weeks.

I wish to say a few words on this question. I am going to make a statement of the -case as it has been given to me and I am subject to correction; although the statements of the minister so far absolutely agree with the statement given me. I fancy therefore that the facts are as stated. The statement, as given to me, is that the tenders were called for in December, 1927. There were some five or six tenders. Canadian Transcontinental Airways Limited was the company which was finally given the contract between Montreal and Father Point, and Montreal and Ottawa. According to the statement given me their figure is $57,500, covering the two contracts, or higher than the contract of the Fairchild people by $17,500. The Fairchild people tendered on a basis which would work out, on the trips for which they tendered, at $40,500. But the contract was as I say, let finally to the Canadian Transcontinental Airways Limited for $57,750.
That includes what routes?

That is Montreal-Father
Point, and Montreal-Ottawa. I am taking these two-
Those figures are right.

Am I right in regard to
the tender of the Fairchild people of $40,500? That is the figure given me, and that is the sum I arrive at on the basis of the tender, a copy of which I looked over.

I would not say from
memory. Had I thought that these figures would be required I would have got them.

I will make a statement
and if the minister finds I am wrong, I shall be subject to correction. If these figures are correct-and I have no reason to doubt their accuracy, because the figures the minister has given absolutely agree so far with these-then there is a loss of some $17,500. I take the Fairchild tender and I shall give in a moment my reasons for doing so. Now the minister pointed out that the air branch of the National Defence department were asked for reports and according to the return which I have seen their recommendation was not so strong for the company to which the contract was given as it was for the Fairchild people. The minister shakes his head as though I were not correct. I will quote the return. I do not wish to take up the time of the committee but the facts should be presented to the house. I have in my hand a letter from Mr. Desbarats, the Deputy Minister of the Department of National Defence dated February 9, 1928, in which he says:
As requested in your letter of February 8, I attach hereto report prepared on the tenders received-
And so forth. This clause affects the situation :
You will note that the Western Canada Airways, the Fairchild Aviation Limited-
That is the one to which I referred.
-Canadian Airways Limited and, perhaps, Canadian Transcontinental Airways Limited-
That is the one to which the contract was finally given.
-are the four companies whose offers are considered likely to give satisfaction in the performance of this contract.
Certainly that paragraph in the letter represents the Canadian Transcontinental Airways Limited as the weakest company of the four. It does not give them a rating as high; it states "and, perhaps, Canadian Transcon-tient-al Airways Limited".
That is not the whole statement ; there is some doubt in that regard.

I do not care what Mr. Desbarats said; we experienced no difficulty with that company in connection with their mail service during the winter season. If ever a company gave satisfaction in carrying on an air mail service this company did so, following air routes just as dangerous as that to Greenly island. Their service along the north shore and the gulf of St. Lawrence and to the Magdalene islands in all kinds of weather; their continuity of service, only missing one trip during the season owing to an accident; their persistent endeavours to give accommodation to the people they served under very trying conditions gave a good deal of satisfaction to t'he department and these were some of the reasons for which I favoured them when the contract was let.

I have no quarrel with what the minister says, but he did quote from the air branch of the Department of National Defence and since he quoted one side of the question I am going to quote the other side.
I quoted them as to the choice of machines we should use, but I did not quote them as to the experience of these people, because I had those details before me.

Very well. I have quoted their views with respect to the company which received the contract; I am a little afraid that in the passage between the minister and myself this may have been forgotten, so I will quote it again:
Aircraft suitable. This company is a new organization with little operating experience. Difficulty is being experienced carrying out present mail contracts.
Now I am going to read what they say about the Fairchild people:
This firm has had five years' operating experience. Aircraft offered are suitable type. Company's main base is well situated for operation of this particular route.
In other words, their recommendation as to the Fairchild people is considerably better than their recommendation of Canadian Transcontinental Airways, the people who received the contract, whom they said were experiencing difficulty in carrying out their present air mail contract.

There has been no difficulty.
Mr, MANION: With all due respect to the minister I doubt if he knows anything more about aircraft than I do, and I admit that is not very much, so I will have to accept the report of the air branch of the Department of National Defence in preference to the opinion of the minister. That is one point. Here was a company recommended by another branch of the government-
What is the date of that report?

It is the same report, dated February 9 last. This company was awarded the contract, and according to this report they are not os well fitted for the work as another company whose tender was not accepted, even though it was for $17,500 less. I do not quite follow the reason of the minister for this action. Then there is another point, more or less a point of ethics. Tenders were called for; I know this is done sometimes in the government and perhaps has happened in the past, but after they were called for they were ignored. Negotiations were carried on between the department and Canadian Transcontinental Airways, whose original tendeT was $1,025 per trip for the Montreal-Father Point trip as against the Fairchild offer of $300. For the Ottawa-Momtreal trip the original tender of these people was $460 as against $75 which was the sum stated by the Fairchild people. So if any negotiations were to be carried on I should have thought they would have been carried on with the Fairchild people. Their tender was not the lowest. I think one or two companies had lower tenders, but I think they were not experienced and were not well reported on. I can quite understand that the lowest tender need not be taken, because we are never bound to do that, but the Fairchild people were reported upon favourably, and I cannot get it through my head-perhaps I am dense-why they should have been ignored, unless there are other reasons which the minister has not yet given, in favour of a company which has not had much experience and which is rather reported against by the air branch of the Department of National Defence. I would be rather glad to hear what the minister has to say.

The hon. gentleman said that perhaps I did not know any more about aircraft than he does, and he said he knew very little about it. Let me say that I do possess a little more knowledge than he showed this afternoon, although I have never done any flying. If I am not mistaken the report from which be was reading was dated
Supply

Post Office

last February. When the final decision was made to aiward this contract we had before us the experience of the company which had been flying during the winter along the north shore and the gulf of St. Lawrence and to the Magdalen islands.
To which company does the minister refer?
I am referring to Canadian Transcontinental Airways Limited.
Can the minister tell us who compose this company?
No, I cannot. I know the names of some of the officials, that is all.
Is this an incorporated company?
Yes, but I do not know who are the directors.
Does my hon. friend know the directors?

No, I do not know the officials except from seeing their names on their letterhead but I know the general manager, Dr. Cuisinier, who offered his services to go to Greenly island and assist in the rescue of the men who flew across from Ireland.
Of course that was subsequent to the giving of the contract.

That was when we were discussing this contract and looking into the whole question. I have had no experience in flying; I doubt whether I would ever go up in an aeroplane, because I feel safer on terra firma. However, -the experience I have was gained from the reports submitted to the department on each trip made during the winter by this company. This service was carried on under very hazardous conditions, and the experience they have had flying this route in winter time is an experience which no other flying company in Canada has had. They carried on their work successfully; at a time when we were up against it to maintain oommiunications which we desired to maintain on the north shore and the gulf of St. Lawrence and especially to the Magdalen islands, they undertook that work for us and have given absolute satisfaction. They have proved that they are fully equipped in every way as far as flying equipment, pilots and mechanicians are concerned. At then- head they have one of the aces of the world war, and I felt that their experience was sufficient to warrant my doing business with them.
(Mr. Veniot.l
I will admit that the minister differs rather materially from the report of the Department of National Defence, because they say this company has had very little experience.

I cannot help that. They began flying in the month of December and flew all winter. They made ten or twelve trips to Seven Islands; several trips to Anticosti; a trip a week to Magdalen islands, and continued that until the opening of navigation. They only missed once towards the end of the season, owing to an accident to their plane. Perhaps at the time Mr. Des-barats made that report they may not have had much experience in flying, but I would like to find one man in Canada who has had more experience than Dr. Cuisinier.

I do not wish to take up much time on this question but my ban. friend leaves himself open to a misunderstanding. He said that up to the time Mr. Desbarats made his report this company may not have had very much experience. Would I assume from that that after Mr. Desbarats made his report they got a good deal of experience?
I told my hon. friend that they commenced flying in the month of December.

But the report of Mr. Desbarats says that the Fairchild Aviation Company has been flying for five years. Mr. Desbarats is a deputy in the Department of National Defence, and this is his report: Fairchild Aviation Company: This firm has had five years' operating experience. Aircraft offered are suitable type. Company's main base is well situated for operation of this particular route.
Another strange thing is that this contract was given after the tenders were called for and the tenders ignored. About three weeks after Mr. Desbarat's report, on March 20, the minister wires to tire company, as follows :
Your wire received. You are in error touching my agreeing to one fifty per mile for your trips Rimouski to Montreal. What I agreed to was four trips at one twenty five or three trips at one fifty, whichever suited you best, the details to be worked out between you and Coolican. Department's most favourable price for Rimouski-Montreal and Montreal-Ottawa total, $57,750.
I am not admitting that; I think the most favourable price was $40,000, according to my figure. The figures were given to me and

Sup-ply-Post Office
I tried to check them up as carefully as possible. The telegram continues:
In view of near approach to opening of navigation, I will have to make other arrangements unless you come to speedy decision. There is no intention of trying to sidetrack your company, but I cannot accept your figures.
And then the negotiations went on, and the minister closed with these people. But in addition to that, while these people only tendered for thirty weeks, which is during the summer, I assume, a contract was given for four years.
Both companies have got a four year contract, for thirty weeks in the year.

If the figures had been
worked out from the original tender, it would show a total of $40,000 for the Fairchild people and $150,000 for the other company, or a difference of $110,000. To show that this company has not done too badly by this contract, I would like to quote from an advertisement appearing in the Financial Post of this week. This is an advertisement for The Canadian Transcontinental Airways Limited, class A stock, which is being offered at $17 per share. I will just quote a couple of clauses, as follows:
The company has already received contracts from the Canadian government covering a number of years' operation. These contracts have been made after the cost per mile of operation for a number of aerial transportation companies in the United States was known. They allow the Canadian Transcontinental Airways Limited, an operating margin which assures large profits. Under the contracts, the company agrees to meet European passenger boats at Father Point.

Does the advertisement
state who they are?
No, it does not; I do not know the names of the officers.

Dr. Cuisimier is one of
them, and he is the one with whom I have had a good deal of communication. I think the legal head of the company is Mr. Robert Cannon.

I notice some of the telegrams were signed by the company and some by the gentleman the minister has just mentioned. It was the hon. gentleman behind me who was asking who were in charge. I would point out that according to the advertisement the company feel they have made a very good contract.
That is not an advertisement of the company you are reading.

It is an advertisement for their shares. Of course, at the bottom appears the usual statement contained in these advertisements:
The statements contained in this advertisement are not guaranteed, but are based upon information, which we believe to be reliable,
That is a broker's advertisement.

They are the financial
agents, and they got their information from the company. It would be illegal for them to do anything else.

In summing up, the following facts would appear: The contract was given out at too high a price, a higher price than that tendered by a company reported as being a better one by the Department of National Defence; a four year contract was given where the tenders called for thirty weeks; negotiations were carried on with these people after calling for tenders, and those who had tendered lower were thrown aside; an opportunity was apparently given to organize a company which, the minister says had a lot of flying experience, but which according to the Department of National Defence lacked experience; and the proposition in the paper for selling stock rather looks as if it were the offering of a new company. The whole thing looks to me as if the minister felt that he should not pay any attention to the tenders, and for one reason or another-I certainly do not impute wrong motives-he went above the price that it was necessary to pay. In these times of high costs I thought the matter was worth taking up, because it seems to me to be an unnecessary waste of money.
Why did you not take up the other company, the Canadian Airways Limited?

To tell you the honest
truth I d'id not happen to have the facts. The minister says tenders weTe called and I will take his word.

The hon. gentleman will

This seems to afford a reasonable opportunity for me to bring to the attention of the committee and the minister the circumstances connected with the dismissal of Mr. J. C. McAdam, who was postmaster at Lafleche, Saskatchewan. As I happen to be the only member of the house on this side from west of the great lakes who apparently could 'be entrusted with the duty of bringing this matter to the attention of the committee, I feel it is a duty devolving upon me to bring up what I consider to be a

Supply-Post Office
great outrage resulting in a grave injustice to a returned soldier who had served in the 10th Battalion, one of the battalions that went earliest to the war, and who was wounded. The circumstances in connection with the matter seem to be as follows. On the 3rd March, 1927, Mr. Thomas Donnelly, member of parliament, wrote from Ottawa to the Postmaster General as follows:
Dear Veniot:
I desire hereby to request the dismissal of Mr. J. C. McAdam, as postmaster at Lafleche, Saskatchewan, for political reasons of which I have personal knowledge.
I will assume all responsibility in this matter, and will answer any questions that may be asked either in the house or outside it, concerning Mr. McAdam's dismissal.
1 desire also hereby to recommend that Mr. Thomas Stark be appointed temporary postmaster in Mr. McAdam's place.
Yours truly,
Thos. Donnelly.
On that there is this notation:
March 4, 1927. Please put this through by order in council. P.J.V.
In due course an order in council was passed, a certified copy of which appears on the file, dismissing Mr. McAdam as postmaster on the ground of his partisanship. The order in council which is dated the 14th March, 1927, reads:
The committee of the privy council, on the recommendation of the Postmaster General advise that the services of Mr. J. C. McAdam, postmaster at Lafleche, Saskatchewan, be dispensed with on the ground of political partisanship.
E. J. Lemaire.
Clerk of the Privy Council.
It is perfectly clear that up to that point the Postmaster General is not blamable. By a standing order in council that was passed, I think in 1911 or 1912, it was provided that if any member of the house certified over his signature that any particular person was an offensive partisan or was guilty of partisanship-
That he has personal knowledge.

Yes, that he had personal knowledge that a particular person was guilty of partisanship in his particular constituency, the minister to whom the letter was directed would, as a matter of course, take steps to have the necessary order in council passed. Up to that point it seems to me that the Postmaster General is not censurable. He merely carried out the conditions of an order in council. But the difficulty began there. As soon as Mr. McAdam knew that he was dismissed-and he was advised that
an order in council had been passed dismissing him-he asked for an investigation. The citizens of the community in which he lived, without his solicitation, gathered together and prepared several petitions which were signed by a very large number of persons, asking that he be retained in his position as postmaster at this village. The postmastership yielded him a livelihood. As a matter of fact the salary, rental of the buildings and the commission gave him between $1,800 and $2,000. The first petition, for instance, is one signed by W. F. Hamelin. general merchant; J. H. Elsey, hardware merchant, and fifty-five other persons. The other one is signed by R. C. Davidson, agent; Alex. Stewart, implement dealer, and1 eighty-six other persons. That is 145 persons signed these two petitions. Then followed another step in this unfortunate transaction. The following telegram was sent to the right hon. the Prime Minister on the 22nd March of this year:
We the undersigned citizens of Lafleche feeling great injustice done to J. C. McAdam in his dismissal from post office here and the appointment of E. H. Bilodeau in his place respectfully request the immediate reconsideration of the matter and thorough investigation of the circumstances leading to Mr. McAdam's dismissal.
That is signed by fifty people or more. According to the return of the last election there was not that number of persons there who voted for a Conservative candidate, nor was there that number of persons who voted for a Progressive candidate, so that it may be taken for granted that of those one hundred and fifty people who signed the petition and the fifty people who signed the telegram to the Prime Minister, a considerable number were neither Conservative nor Progressives but must have been supporters of the present administration. My contention is this, that when a returned man, finding himself charged with offensive partisanship denies that there is any truth in the charge; when he asks and demands that there should be an investigation, and when a number of citizens, some fifty in this particular instance, take the trouble to send a telegram to the prime Minister asking for an investigation, that investigation should be granted.
I may point out that on the file brought down, there was lacking a letter which was in my judgment rather an important one, namely, the letter written by Mr. McAdam himself to the Postmaster General. That letter does not appear on the file, the reason probably being that they did not ask the minister for his personal file on the matter.

That is the only reason.

Having had something
to do with the dismissal of this postmaster at Lafleche, I feel that I should explain my action. Let me preface what I have to say by the statement that the constituency of Willow Bunch was only surveyed in 1908, and1 the first road was built through it in 1910 or 1911. After that time, postmasters were appointed in all the towns of any size along that line, and no political partisanship was used in their appointment because our friends the Conservatives were in power at that time; yet strange to say, all the postmasters in towns of any importance throughout the constituency are Conservatives, only one postmastership in a town of any size being held by a Liberal, and the reason assigned for him being appointed, I am told, is that they could not find a Conservative in the place to appoint.
I am in the fortunate or unfortunate position, being a medical man and travelling through that district, of knowing pretty well the political views of everybody out there. In the 1925 and 1926 elections I had the misfortune or good fortune to hear Mr. McAdam on several occasions trying to influence voters by speaking against myself, against the Prime Minister of this country, and against the Liberal party. After the 1925 election, being a new man in politics, I did not say anything about it. In 1926, he acted in the same way, and these men were going around saying, "The Civil Service Commission appoints us, and no one can discharge us." I thought it was time to show them that if they were going to indulge in politics they could not hold a government job. So I made representations, as is shown by the letter, that Mr. McAdam had been politically active, and I advised that he be dismissed.
I notice what was said with regard to the petition. I heard only two names. A delegation came up to see me with regard to this man's dismissal, and two of those men were in the delegation. They admitted that Mr. McAdam had no one to blame but himself, for he had been politically active, there was no doubt about that, but they said he had been a pretty good postmaster-I knew that-and having now been taught his lesson he should be forgiven and taken back. I told them it was too late to lock the door after the horse was stolen-the matter was in the hands of the Civil Service Commission, that I had no love for him, and as I had heard him talking against myself, against the party and against the Prime Minister, as far as I was concerned the dismissal would stand.
With regard to the appointment of Mr. Bilodeau, I advised that Mr. Stark be put in as temporary postmaster. He refused to take the job. The Civil Service Commission, I understand, appointed a Mr. Scott. He too was a returned soldier, but he had moved away from the town to another place further north and refused to come back. Later I am informed the Civil Service Commission appointed Mr. Bilodeau, who is in temporary charge as postmaster. Some organizations through that district, such as the Klu Klux Klan and the Orange order, objected very much to this, because they said: Here is a Protestant, a returned soldier, being turned out of a job and a Frenchman and Catholic being put in his place. Not being a Frenchman or a Catholic myself, religion does not influence me at all. I believe a man has a right to whatever religion he professes. But even at that I do not think Mr. McAdam has very much coming to him. During the last election I had a Frenchman and Catholic running against me, and Mr. McAdam did everything he could to elect that Frenchman and Catholic. He was beaten by the fortunes of war, and I think he should take his medicine.

The hon. gentleman said he heard Mr. McAdam attack himself and the Liberal party and the Prime Minister. That in my judgment would be clear evidence of partisanship, if he was then postmaster, and within the provisions of the order in council of 1912. I strongly deprecate the question that the hon. member has seen fit to introduce. In all the letters I have received I find nothing about the religion of Mr. McAdam or of anyone connected with him. Neither do I find any reference made to the racial origin or religion of the person who is now postmaster. In fact I may say that one of my correspondents is himself a leading Roman

inst. will be accepted, and that all failing to resume their duties by that hour will be definitely refused thereafter a place in the federal service. Commencing at the above stated hour new employees will be engaged on the usual permanent basis.

The reappointment of the striker must have the approval of the governor in council:
On reappointment, the striker must give satisfactory assurances that there will not be a repetition of the offence:
The striker must pass the ordinary Civil Service Commission examination and he must commence anew in the service.
These regulations have been in force since the fall of 1919 or the spring of 1920. There were 416 permanent employees and 267 temporary employees dismissed by order in council for failing to return to work after the ultimatum had been issued. I would draw the attention of the committee to the fact that the ultimatum was delivered on Saturday, a public holiday, and required the return of the workers by twelve o'clock on the following Monday. There have been a number of ex-strikers retaken on the staffs of the various post offices. There are now seventy-two ex-strikers on the staff of the Winnipeg post office, two at Saskatoon, mine at Calgary and four at Vancouver. When these men were taken back into the government employ they were put on the jobs they formerly held; they were required to do work which they had been doing prior to their dismissal consequent upon going out on dtrike. These men were experienced in the work of the post office; they bad training and they had shown themselves to be competent men. The figures will show that at the time of their going out on strike, their average length of service was seven years. That is, the majority of the men who are now in the service of the government had put in, at the time of their dismissal, seven years service with the government. They had training and experience in post office matters.

Supply-Post Office
When these men were taken back they were put on their old jobs. Those who had been sorting mail, were put back at sorting; those who had delivered mail, were put back on delivering; those who had been supervisors, were put back at supervising, and those who had been clerks, or had served in capacities requiring experience, were put back in those positions as vacancies occurred. But when these men were taken back they were paid as postal helpers, the lowest grade known to the post office, and some of them are still being paid as postal helpers. The Dominion government has taken advantage of their training, of their experience, and of their services in the respective classes to which they belong, and yet has only paid them as postal helpers. There is one case in the city of Winnipeg of an ex-striker holding a position as supervisor, and having under him four or five men who were not strikers. The four or five men under him were receiving the maximum salary while the supervisor, being an exnstriker, was receiving the salary of a podtal helper.
I would not approve of this vote if it justified the strike in any way. I think there has been a good deal of nonsense spoken with regard to the strike. I think at this time we can view the strike and what happened very calmly and dispassionately. It has not been suggested that this item involves a justification of the strike; it does no such thing. If it involved a justification of the strike I would not have approved of it. The men who have been taken back have freely admitted that they were badly advised in going out on strike, and they have undertaken that there will be no repetition of the occurrence in so far as they themselves are concerned. This proposal does not involve the reinstatement of striking employees; it does not involve the restoration of seniority right. It is necessary to keep faith with the men who took the places of the strikers, and no man who is now in the Winnipeg post office or in any of the post offices affected by this vote is going to lose any rights of seniority. He will not be prejudiced in any way, and he will not lose the position he occupies. While it is necessary to keep faith with the men who occupied the places of the ex-strikers, it is also necessary that this committee and the parliament of Canada should recognize the great principle that services should be paid for according to their value. That is all that is involved in this vote, namely, that we should pay these men in accordance with the services which they rendered to the post office. Nothing else is involved in this vote except the
56103-25SJ
preservation and application of that great principle and those who have been advocating that this be done, have done so with a desire to see applied to these men the elementary principles of justice of which the leader of the opposition spoke this afternoon. This is not a justification for the strike.
It is a palliation.

It is not an attempt to
reinstate the rights of seniority that were forfeited and lost through going out on strike. The role and only purpose of this vote is to pay the striking employees of the post office who are back again in the public service in accordance with the value of the services which they were rendering. It is not giving them something to which they are not entitled. They have already earned what it is now proposed to pay them. There is a great principle involved. Since the Dominion government has taken these men back into the government service, the Dominion government should pay them in accordance with the value of the services rendered. I could quite well understand the position that might be taken that the Dominion government should never take these men back. That would be a perfectly understandable position to take and there would be some justification for it. But once having taken these men back into the public service, and having used their services, the Dominion government should follow-the example of other employers and pay these men according to the value of their services.

It perhaps will clarify
and simplify the discussion to ask: Are they not being paid according to the terms of the contract of their employment when they went back?

I am glad the leader'
of the opposition has asked that question. It is a pertinent question to ask. But let me answer it by asking him another question. Many of these men had been in the service of the Post Office Department for ten or fifteen years; they were not fitted or qualified for other kinds of work; there was an odium attached in the city of Winnipeg to all exstrikers, and they found it difficult to get employment. I ask the leader of the opposition whether it was a fair offer to these men to say to them: We will take advantage of your services; we will take advantage of the fact that you have been for many years in
Business of the House

the service of the Post Office Department; but we will make the best bargain with you that we can, and we will take you back as apprentices?
What was the bargain?

I have been attempting
to indicate the bargain and I have already indicated to the committee the terms -upon which the men were reemployed. But what I am saying with respect to that is that that was a very unfair condition to attach to the reemployment, because it was taking advantage of the situation in which the men were placed.
Who put them there?

It took advantage of
the situation in which the men were placed. The Dominion government is the only employer of labour that has acted in that particular way.
I have a telegram saying that the opposite is the case.

Let me continue with
my argument. Other employers pf labour have in some instances refused to take back striking employees. That is a perfectly understandable position to take, but when they did take them back they paid them at the current rate of wages. If, for instance, an iron master took back a mechanic, he paid him the wages that were payable to a mechanic. He did not pay him the wages that an apprentice would receive; he paid him as a mechanic and not as an apprentice. But the Dominion government, taking advantage of the position in which the men were placed, .stated that they would take them back only -as apprentices. Yet when they did take them back they put them in positions that they Rad formerly occupied; they used their services, their training, their experience. The suggestion that is made in this vote is that even at this late date justice should be done and the men should be paid in accordance with the value of the services rendered by them.
And Mr. Speaker having resumed the chair.

Mr. Speaker, before we leave
private bills I desire to say I cannot 'but think that matters so vitally affecting the business

I do not propose in any sense to express an opinion with regard to the bills, but I do say we must in some way amend our rules or modify our procedure to prevent that situation recurring. It is bad for the country, it is bad for parliament, and it is worse for the commercial community whose interests may be affected. I have not a word to say in criticism of those who do not approve of measures and desire to discuss them, but a minority of twenty or twenty-five should never bo able to prevent a vote being taken and the will of the house recorded. If this house is in favour of the legislation it should have the opportunity to so declare; if the house disapproves, there should be an opportunity afforded to so record itself.
I venture to make these observations at the end of this session because I have not heretofore said anything with respect to the matter. I do hope we may be able to arrive at some method by which a recurrence of the situation may be prevented. Vote 519, supplementary estimates.
Post office - outside service - salaries and allowances-further amount required to hereby adjust the salaries of former permanent post office employees who were dismissed from the postal service on account of their participation in the postal strike of 1919, and who have since been re-employed and are still in the service, such adjustment to give the employees the benefit of the salary they would have received had they re-entered the service in the class equivalent to the one in which they were formerly placed, and also of the salary revisions of 1919 and 1924, in which they would

Supply-Post Office
have participated had they remained in the service, notwithstanding anything to the contrary in the Civil Service Act, $115,000.
Purchase of rural mail boxes-further amount required, $40,000.
Mail service by air and land conveyance, including rural mail delivery-further amount required, $150,000.

Mr. Chairman, I do not
propose to occupy the time of the committee very much longer. The hon. leader of the opposition put certain questions to me with regard to the conditions under which the striking postmen had been readmitted to employment. The position which I suggest should be taken in regard to that is that these men were not able to choose between employments. They were quite ready, from the fact that they had not been employed and had not been able to get employment, to take any employment that offered,' no matter what terms were imposed. But, Mr. Chairman, the position I take is this. The condition that these men should be paid as new men seems a very unfair condition to attach to their reemployment; that condition now should be changed and full justice should be done these men. They should be paid in accordance with the value of the services rendered. Every other employer who has taken back into his employ men who went on strike has paid these men full value for their services; the Dominion government has been the only exception to that rule, and I suggest that it is not too late for this government to remedy the injustice which was done. These men who went on strike and who have been reemployed by the Dominion government were not vicious men; a large number of them were returned soldiers and they had all contributed their share to the patriotic fund and had done their part in looking after the welfare of the returned men. They had performed their duties conscientiously and well. Perhaps they were misled, but at any rate they have promised that they will not take part in a strike of this nature again, so there is no danger of a recurrence of the trouble in the future. Many of these men lost their homes and their savings before they were re-admitted into the service for which they were trained and for which they were well qualified.
This request that justice be done these men does not come from them alone; it has the support of many bodies and groups of men. The Winnipeg postal group, by a very large vote, have endorsed this proposal, although only a small portion of that group are exstrikers; the Amalgamated Civil Servants of Winnipeg have also endorsed the suggestion,
as have the executive of the Canadian Legion in that city. This is not a new proposal in the history of Canada. There are precedents for the suggestion now made, precedents which were just and which we should follow in this case. In 1924 the postmen of Toronto went out on strike; they were sent an ultimatum similar to that given the Winnipeg strikers. Then they were dismissed and told that they would not be reemployed. However, they were reemployed on the same terms as those offered to the Winnipeg strikers, as vacancies occurred and as new employees. In 1926 the Dominion government realized the justice of their claim and reinstated them, going further than it is now proposed to go and giving them their back pay, recognizing the justice of that procedure. It would be interesting to know the attitude of the leader of the opposition in connection with this proposal and to know whether his attitude is shared by some of his colleagues. I am sorry the hon. member for Fort William is not in his seat; I have been told that when he was touring Manitoba during the last election he met a group of these men. They placed their case before him and he expressed sympathy with their application. They told him about the Toronto strike and what had been done there, and I am told that on that occasion after hearing their representations he stated that if the Conservatives were returned to power and if he remained Postmaster General he would be prepared to treat them as the striking postmen in Toronto had been treated. If I am incorrectly advised I hope the hon. member will put me right.
I make this suggestion because I believe it to be just and proper; I believe if we adopt it we will remedy a wrong which has existed in Winnipeg for a long time and heal a sore which has been festering for years. No one is being prejudiced; no justification of the strike is involved; we are merely recognizing the fact that the Dominion of Canada should pay these men according to the value of the service rendered. I suggest that this committee adopt this item so that now, after this long lapse of time, justice may be done and a fitting end written to one of the most distressing chapters in the history of Winnipeg.

Nine years ago last April a delegation of Winnipeg postal employees representing the entire body of men employed in the post office of that city visited Ottawa, the capital of Canada. They met a delegation of the then cabinet. They were asked
40S8
Supply-Post Office

as to their grievances and they indicated slight changes which they desired to have made in the terms of their employment. Their wishes were met in full and when they left this city to return to Winnipeg they left behind them letters of thanks directed to the ministers in question, thanking them for the courteous way in which they had been received and for the willingness shown by the government of the day to meet every just claim they had to make. They stated that they had no complaints of any kind to make with respect to the terms of their employment, the conditions of their service or their relation to their employers, who were the people of Canada.
Just about a month thereafter some 480 of the Winnipeg postal employees left their employment; they left without notice; they left without providing substitutes; they left without any personal grievances or any complaints as to their service or the conduct of their employers. They left the service of the state in violation of their oaths of office as public servants of the Dominion of Canada, and the reason they gave for leaving the public service were that a strike had been called by certain men in that city, and an effort was being made to establish a Soviet form of government in Winnipeg. An additional reason given was that some of them were compelled by intimidation to leave their employment.
Let us consider just what that means. If we can only approach this matter in a spirit somewhat different from that of the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat after endeavouring to make political capital out of it, I think perhaps it would be more to the advantage of this country.
What justification has the leader of the opposition for making that statement?
Just the language used by the hon, gentleman himself, and nothing more.
I think that statement should be withdrawn.

His language is opon to only one inference, the only inference that would be drawn by any court. He himself is a member of the profession; he assisted in the prosecution of those who originated the effort to establish a Soviet in the city of Winnipeg. He was one of the prosecuting counsel, and I ask him to say to this house whether or not he thinks the conviction obtained in one of these cases was improperly obtained? An appeal was taken to the Privy 
Council, which declined to allow it because, while the Privy Council only in rare cases hears appeals from criminal convictions, the lord chancellor at that time made it perfectly clear that it was apparent, after a most exhaustive statement of the case by learned counsel, that there had been no departure from the principles that govern the administration of criminal law in every part of the British Empire, in the trial and conviction of at least one of these offenders. Does the hon. gentleman who spoke this [DOT]afternoon say to this house that this man was improperly convicted?

I propose to answer that
question. I made it perfectly clear to this house that if this vote had implied justification of the strike, I would have opposed it. No justification of the strike is involved in the vote. I-

My hon. friend knows better than to do that. He will have his chance, and I shall proceed now with my observations. I have permitted him to give an answer.

You asked me a question.
Mr.. BENNETT:	I asked a question and
the hon. member has answered it. He has said that if this vote involved in any sense approval of the strike he would not have supported the measure. I therefore think that if I can show to the committee that the vote does imply that very thing, the hon. member will withdraw his support of the item in the estimates. This trial having proceeded, as I have said, the conviction having been made and sustained by the court of last resort in the British Empire, we have then a just and proper conviction for an effort to establish another form of government in Canada.

Will the hon.
gentleman permit a question? In what way can he say that the decision of the courts * in Winnipeg was upheld by the Privy Council? '

An application was made for leave to appeal to the Privy Council. The case was presented by learned counsel not only of the English but of the Winnipeg bar; and the Privy Council, after listening to the argument, indicated that there was no cause shown for hearing the appeal, and leave was refused.

Did the Privy
Council listen to the argument?

The hon. gentlemen who presented the case to the Privy Council is now one of the learned judges of the court of appeal of Manitoba. He presented his argument for the better part of a day. The Privy Council listened with great attention and at the end of the discussion the lord chancellor-if my memory serves me it was the lord chancellor of the day-gave judgment, declaring that no case had been made out indicating that the conviction was wrong either in law or otherwise, or that it offended the principles and canons of justice that prevail throughout the British Empire in relation to criminal cases, and therefore the conviction would not be quashed by the Privy Council.

Was it not true
that refusal of the Privy council to consider the matter was based on constitutional grounds?

It is hardly correct to
say that it, was based on constitutional grounds. It was based on this large ground: that no case had been made out that would warrant interference by the Privy Council. When I say that no case was made out I mean that there was no such departure from the principles of justice that govern all criminal trials in the British Empire as would warrant interference by the Privy Council in rehearing or considering the case. In other words, what the Privy Council said, by the judgment of the lord chanceller, was that the principles of justice had been observed in the trial, that the evidence warranted the conviction, that the conviction was sound in law and therefore must stand. That was the judgment of the Privy Council. The constitutional question to which the hon. member refers is a simple one: it was whether or not the Privy Council would consider a criminal appeal. The Privy Council has considered criminal appeals and has since that time declared that where there is any departure from the principles of justice that govern all British courts in criminal trials, the case will be considered by the Privy Council. Those are the facts.
We have therefore a conviction which, to the hon. gentleman who has just spoken, must appear a sound conviction. We have a conviction because an effort was made to destroy the established form of government of this country in the city of Winnipeg. In other words, an effort was made to change our government and that effort failed.
Supply-Post Office

Would the hon. leader
suggest by that statement, that all who took part in the strike of 1919 in Winnipeg had that intention in mind?

It is hardly necessary to
answer a question of that kind, and it is not expected that a lawyer will answer it. It is not expected that one of the profession would ask so simple a question.
Answer it.

I am not here to give
instruction in law to the hon. gentleman; it might pay for him to sit somewhere and learn a little. But I do not propose to give that instruction at the moment.
The conviction having been made because of an effort, mark you, to destroy the government of Canada in the province of Manitoba and in the city of Winnipeg, and that effort having failed, one of our citizens, was prosecuted, and convicted. It will be found in the law reports of the country. Now what relation has that to this vote?
None.

It is necessary for the
hon. gentleman to say none if he desires to retain his position as having a logical mind. However, I shall show that it has a very direct bearing on the matter. Let us bear in mind my opening observation: 480 men who had no direct grievance of their own, had left the postal service of Canada without notice, in violation of their oath. They left, not because they had any grievance of their own, because they admitted they had none. But citizens one of whom was subsequently convicted as I have indicated, were endeavouring to establish another form of government in Canada, a soviet in the city of Winnipeg. The government was confronted with that situation-a complete tie-up in the postal service. What does it mean to the commercial life of Canada and to the domestic life of our citizens to have a complete postal tie-up? Business was paralyzed, the postal service was discontinued, no deliveries made of letters to homes. The people were without communication so far as the postal service was concerned-absolutely without it. The government of the day permitted that condition to continue, urging as best they could, that there should be a settlement of these difficulties. Time went on; two weeks passed; and then the Minister of Labour of Canada, the Honourable Gideon Robertson,-and I think, although my memory may be wrong,
Supply-Post Office

the Right Honourable Arthur Meighen-went to Winnipeg. The first thing they did was, not to endeavour to coerce the postal clerks, but to ask them whether they had any grievances against this country, their employer. They admitted they had none. They were not on strike because any wrong had been done to them personally, but because they were in sympathy with those who were endeavouring to destroy the government of Canada. The relation between the conviction and the sympathy is found in the fact that that effort to destroy the government was held to be criminal, and one of them was convicted under the conditions to which I have referred. Therefore, the sympathy was for a criminal act, an act which was declared by the court of last resort to be criminal; that is clear. I think this answers the question asked by the hon. gentleman. There is the answer; it was sympathy for a criminal conspiracy, a conspiracy to destroy the government of Canada.
What, did the government of the country do? Mark you, the government, after all, is but a trustee for the whole population of Canada. I was not in the house at that time, so I can speak with some freedom with respect to the matter; I was not even in politics. The position was a very simple one. Confronted with the paralysis of the postal service of Canada for. upwards of two weeks; no mail; business being ruined, and homes without letters, what 'happened? The then Minister of Labour, and the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen on Friday gave public notice through the papers, and by personal notice, directed to all those who were concerned, through the, postmaster, pointing out that the postal employees were acting in violation of their oath of public service, and the public service must be resumed. That was a clear and frank recognition that all men may act hastily, and of the influence of the mass over individuals. This was a recognition of what I believe some philosophers call mass psychology ; the influence of the many over the mind of the individual. It has a clear recognition that men may act hastily and make mistakes; that they may be guilty of errors of judgment. The leader of the opposition went into a rolling series of sentences with regard to the effort to establish a soviet form of government in Winnipeg, and all this kind of thing. Yet he also stated in another connection that these men were sitting in conference discussing their grievances. Do you suppose that men who were trying to overturn the government of Canada would be sitting listening to the higher officials of the Post Office Department? Why, it is absurd. At the very time the newspapers were sending telegrams out regarding the terrible conditions in Winnipeg, Mr. A. B. Hudson, at one time a member of this house, and several gentlemen were trying to find sonie sort of formula which would settle the trouble with the machinists, which formed the basis of the strike, and thus settle the whole matter.
A good many of the men who were associated with the strikers were returned soldiers. Thousands of returned men just back from the front, who had been labour people before they went abroad and who had found it difficult to secure work, and learned that many of the things for which they had fought were not being worked out here in Canada, associated themselves with the workers. Do you mean to tell me that these thousands of returned men were going to attempt to overturn the government of Canada? The whole thing is preposterous.
For which they had been fighting.

For which they had been fighting. I say the idea is preposterous, and yet these stories were spread across the country. It is quite true that the Hon. G. D. Robertson came to Winnipeg and tried to settle the strike. The trouble is he went at it the wrong way. Had he not come I have not the slightest doubt the city of Winnipeg and the province of Manitoba would have settled it in a much more satisfactory way than it ultimately was settled. But he came in his own peculiar fashion and stirred things up still more, and then he refused to receive a deputation of returned men who waited upon him; he would not let them march to the Royal Alexandra. It was that which caused the trouble that brought about the unfortunate incident in which there was shooting in the streets of Winnipeg.

Did my hon. friend say
that Mr. Meighen refused to receive a deputation of returned men?
It was Mr. Robertson ; I did not say Mr. Meighen.

Was he informed that it
was merely a deputation of returned men?

He was informed
that a procession of returned men wished to wait upon him at the Royal Alexandra, and he refused to see them. He did receive a small committee of these men, and this is what occurred so far as I am able to learn, and I was there and watching it very closely. The returned men said they were going to have a parade whether the Minister of Labour wanted it or not. They had been used to parading in France and they said they intended to have one in Canada. The labour men tried to dissuade them because they recognized the danger of such a parade on the streets at the time of public excitement. However, the returned men said they were going on with it. As a matter of fact, the parade did not even form up, but a great many people came out to see the show. It was a most regrettable occurrence; you would have thought a great circus was coming to town, and the streets were lined in every direction by curious crowds. When the time came for the parade the mayor read the riot act, and then the police came on the scene. There had 'been specials there who had antagonized the people by the way they had handled the crowds. There were some missiles thrown, and then there was the charge and the shooting. That is what occurred.
As I said in this house on one other occasion, if this was to be a physical revolution for the overturn of the government of this country, can you imagine for a moment that the workers would not have armed themselves? In all the investigations that were held there was not found one single gun in the hands of the workers. The idea of a physical revolution being brought about by the strikers in Winnipeg was absolutely preposterous.
I do not think I could do better, to illustrate the kind of hysteria which prevailed, even among our legal friends and the government officials at that time, than by reading a few words from some things I wrote in those days, and for which I was arrested.

How did they find
you?

They found me
when I undertook to edit a paper in the place of a friend of mine who was arrested. I knew pretty nearly what was likely to happen and it did happen. I was arrested, but generally

a man is arrested on regular charges. This was one of the charges on which I was arrested:
The jurors aforesaid do further present:
4. That J. S. Woodsworth, in or about the month of June, in the year of our Lord One thousand nine hundred and nineteen, at the city of Winnipeg, in the province of Manitoba, unlawfully and seditiously published seditious libels in the words and figures following:
"Woe unto them that decree unrighteous decrees, and that write grievousness which they have prescribed: to turn aside the need from judgment, and to take away the right from the poor of my people, that widows may be their prey and that they may rob the fatherless."
Isaiah (110:1-2)
And they shall build houses and inhabit them: and they shall plant vineyards, and eat the fruit of them. They shall not build and another inhabit; they shall not plant and another eat; for as the days of a tree are the days of my people; and mine elect shall long enjoy the work of their hands.
Isaiah (65:21-22)
That was sedition, according to the authorities at that time. I do not think I could give a better illustration of the positive hysteria which prevailed at that time. Do you think men could have a fair trial under those conditions? As far as the law is concerned I also call this to the attention of the leader of the opposition: My hpn. friend from Winnipeg South Centre, who was engaged in the prosecution of these cases, assures me that if my case had actually come to trial he feels quite confident they could have convicted me for having published these two passages.
Let me read in the few moments that remain to me a few paragraphs from the second count of the indictment:
What is the present situation? The sixth week of the strike leaves neither side in control; Both the strike committee and the "citizens" committee are determined to hold out. Neither is by any means at the end of its resources. In the ranks there is little sign of weakening. The strike may be prolonged for weeks. In the _ meantime the business men claim that the city is being ruined-is ruined and the workers undoubtedly will face the winter with reserves sadly depleted.
The City Council, the provincial government or the federal government have adopted no constructive policy. They stood prepared only for repressive measures.
When finally it did seem that the provincial government might effect a settlement, the Dominion government upset everything by its outrageous arrest of the strike leaders.
In the meantime, the returned soldiers are becoming restless and threatening to take things into their own hands. They are tired of the policy of "do nothing"-"keep order", so consistently followed by the strike leaders.
And a little further on:
Mediation, by a body as well equipped as any that is likely to be found, has apparently failed. There is a dead-lock.
What will happen? How will it end? Is there any possible way out?
Members, both of the strikers' committee and the citizens' committee say: "We must fight to a finish. We cannot afford to yield. If it takes three months, we will see it through," ...
I could go on through the whole of that article, which was a conciliatory article written after consultation with some of the leading business men in Winnipeg. I suggested that a commission should be appointed, and that in the meantime the work of the city should go on. I proceed to quote:
The task of such a commission would not be an easy one. The strike has revealed how widely divergent are the views of the employers and "the workers". Then, what is the alternative? A wide bridge must be found or "It's a fight to a finish," and then what?
Let us reiterate there are very reasonable men in both camps.
I said that at a time that, we were all liable to be arrested; I pleaded for mediation at a time when feeling was running high. That is on record and, in passing, I would note that it is curious that that very article should have been one of those said to be seditious. I have not read it all, but any hon. member is welcome to do so.
I have not very much more time to-night. I had not thought to go into this matter at all, but the issue has been forced by the leader of the opposition. I feel that he has been misinformed; he confesses that he has read official documents and he has read the newspapers, but I think I may claim to have been a little nearer the workers. Fundamentally, however, some of the same difficulties are in existence to-day as there were in 1919. Groups of men who occupy prominent positions in the community are accustomed to running things in their own way. I have called attention in this house to the fact that we have a very few people who, through interlocking directorates, control the whole situation. They do not brook any interference or opposition, and when outsiders begin to organize the workers or the farmers immediately they are up in arms. One of the leaders in the United States said only a few weeks ago, "If you wish to damage your opponent do not begin to argue against him but call him a bolshevist; that is the easiest way." That was done in 1919, and I hope the time will yet come when we may have a chance before some impartial tribunal to bring out all of the facts in connection with that struggle.
Now I come back to the postal workers. What are we going to do? I say that a great many of the citizens of Canada have found out in the last nine years how ill-founded were their fears and how one-sided were the sources of their information. I am not tiying

to whitewash the workers; they may have [DOT]made mistakes, but I will say that if they made mistakes there were other, much stronger powers much more lacking in the fundamentals of constitutionalism. I am not a constitutionalist, because I believe that generally you have to initiate things outside the regular lines of constitution. On the other hand I am not one who advocates violent revolution; I have said that before and I have been bitterly condemned for so saying.
The hon. gentleman's time is up.

As I sit down I
would plead for fair play for these strikers.

When this item was first
placed before the committee of supply it was my intention to then make the statement which I wish to now make. When I saw that there was a disposition to discuss the merits of this item I thought perhaps it would not be right to make my statement at that time. Let me say here that for over a year I have given this question serious, deep thought and study. I did not recommend to the government the insertion of this item of SI 15,000 in the supplementary estimates without having given it serious consideration. I cannot agree with those who say that because we would recognize what I considered at that time to be an injustice we are recognizing at the same time the results which developed from the strike of 1919. I know nothing of the Winnipeg strike; I do not want to know anything about the merits or demerits of it. I considered the case as I found it, and since I find in reading the press lately and in the speeches made on the floor of this house that wittingly or unwittingly the case has been misrepresented in many respects, I think it only fair that I should be allowed a few moments to lay the case before the committee as I found it.
The statement that these men were taken back under certain conditions is true, but it is equally true that these conditions were never fulfilled. These men were taken back; they had to undergo a civil service examination in order to qualify, which examination entitled them to be placed in the lowest classification of the service. They should have been placed in that classification and given an opportunity under the merit system to work up to the higher classification which they occupied before the strike. That was not done. When they underwent the civil service examination and were put in the low classification. receiving the wages or salaries of the lower classification, to my mind they should

have been kept there. When they went back into the civil service after passing that examination they were placed in a higher classification and called upon not only to do the work of the more highly classified officials which they were before the strike, but also to instruct the new men who came into the service and to help by their efforts to make the service more efficient.
And at a lower salary.

Yes, at a lower salary, at
the minimum salary. That is where I find the injustice, I am not going to criticize the Postmaster General or the government of that day at all. That is not my intention. I state this merely because I want the facts laid before the country so that there will be no longer any misrepresentation. The case of these men may not end here; it may come up again, and it is for that reason, finding as I have found arguments based upon misrepresentations of this case that I wish to place these facts now before the committee. There having been so much misrepresentation; there having been so much propaganda for and against taking the Winnipeg strikers back; that having been carried on for a certain number of years without anyone having had the opportunity or perhaps the courage to lay the facts exactly as they are before the people; knowing that there is still a very bitter feeling in this matter; that there is still a strong opposition in the house coming from sources where perhaps the case is not well understood; feeling that before I go further in the matter I should give the house a greater opportunity of investigating and examining into the case and not ask it to take this action at this late hour when we are about to prorogue; and feeling that this case will perhaps come up at some later date, I thought I should ask one of my colleagues to move that the vote be reduced by the amount provided for salaries and allowances, namely $115,000. But I want it distinctly understood that I am not doing so on the arguments advanced in the house to-night in that regard, because many of those arguments were not founded upon fact. I do not say that there was intentional misrepresentation; I do not wish to insinuate anything of the kind, but I have the facts before me. I may also point out that I would not withdraw from the case because of a veiled threat that this house might be called upon to sit for several days yet. I will now ask my colleague to move in the matter.

Mr. Chairman, the item
of $525,000 for the purchase of property on Sussex street refers to property known as the New Edinburgh mills. I wish very briefly to state certain facts, and then to submit to the government that they should give this matter further consideration before making the expenditure. In 1924 the pur-
