chase of this property was under consideration, . and the government declined to proceed with it.
My point is briefly stated in the following terms. In the first place the value of the property to the government is as vacant property only. That is the only justification for buying the property. On this property there has been erected a very large and extensive concrete and brick sawmill, box factory and woodworking plant. Obviously, this plant is of no use to the government at all. Unquestionably it was a costly plant to erect, and undoubtedly there still remains in it, as a woodworking plant, a very substantial value. The value is set by two very highly qualified valuators, Messrs. H. Gale Legg and A. E. Cross. Their valuation is well done, and I have no criticism of it. Briefly stated, these are the values:	Land, $135,000; buildings,
$475,000; I submit to the committee, however, that the only value we should consider is the land value, not the building value, because these buildings are of little, use for the purposes suggested.
What is the water-power value?

I cannot go into details,
but I will say this, hydro-electric power is available in constant form so cheaply that I doubt the value of the water-power as an economical unit in connection, with the matter. The assessment is $178,000 on the land and $230,000 on the buildings. In the agreement to purchase will be found the following clause, and I wish to call this particularly to the attention of the government:
The party of the second part in consideration of the covenants and agreements hereinbefore entered into and on the part of the party of the first part to be done and performed, promises and agrees that and so soon as the parliament of Canada shall have appropriated a sufficient sum for that purpose, to accept delivery to them of the aforesaid conveyances and moveable property and take possession thereof with the lands and premises herein described, and to pay forthwith to the party of the first part the sum of $525,000. . .
It is mutually agreed by and between the parties hereto that should the parliament of Canada not appropriate the said sum at its present session, these presents shall at the conclusion of said session become null and void and of no effect.
My point is that the property at the present time is only under option, and while it might appear that by the passing of this estimate the government was irrevocably committed,
I submit it still may retire from the purchase if so desired. A further point is that a part of this property is a lease of Green island, which is the property of the government. The 
building referred to by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) the other day as the one to be used for the statistical bureau is on the end of Green island. I have the lease of Green island under my hand, given by this government in 1904, being a renewal of a longstanding lease. In that lease is a clause reading as follows:
And that if the said demised premises or any portion thereof be required for any purpose which the minister may deem to be in the public interest, possession of the same may at any time during the said period be resumed by His Majesty, his successors or assigns upon six months' notice in writing by the minister to the lessee to that effect, and in no such case shall the lessee have any claim to compensation on account of damage in any way resulting from such resumption or from the deternfination of this demise; but that the lessee may remove, within a reasonable time, any building or buildings which belong to or which may have been erected by it on the demised premises.
In other words, there is on this island a building which it is proposed to remodel and use for the statistical branch. I submit to the minister that he need pay nothing for that as this lease protects the government in that regard.
One further word in connection with the cost. I claim, Mr. Chairman, some knowledge of this class of business. It is in the line I have followed for many years, valuating property and so on. I have examined the property carefully, having in mind the statement of the Minister of Trade and. Commerce the other day, and I submit this: It will cost . from $150,000 to $200,000 expenditure on this property to make it suitable for the purposes suggested the other day-a statistical branch and national research bureau. There is no heating provided; no sanitary accommodation; there are just concrete pillars with a curtain wall of brick. The buildings are well constructed for woodworking but are not suitable for an office or as official buildings. They are not built for that; they are not suitable for the purpose at all, and I submit to the Prime Minister and his government that it will cost more to put these buildings into shape than it would take to construct another building back of Wellington street which could better house the statistical branch and give better service to parliament. I conclude with this one observation: I think it is possible and desirable to secure the lands for the purposes of beautifying that extent of the river to Rockcliffe park. If that is in mind, the land is suitable and desirable for the purpose. But its maximum value would be under $200,000. The buildings on that property, having that use in view, are merely an

That is the maximum; what about the minimum?
That is the minimum; the maximum would probably be between two and three times that amount.
Is the power lease sold?

Eight hundred horsepower of it was leased at $22 per horsepower. There can be no question that for the purposes for which the government require the property, these power rights and the machinery in connection with them are worth at least $200,000.
Where do you get a maximum of two to three times your minimum?
If my hon. friend wishes I will give the figures.
Do you increase your depth some way?

Perhaps I had better make a statement to the committee: For some years the Gatineau Power Company, Limited, supplied the Ottawa Electric Company, from power house erected on these lands, with 800 horsepower at the rate of $2 per horsepower per month bringing in a revenue of $1,600 per month or at the rate of $19,200 per annum. The Gatineau Company have developed and used power up to 1,500 horsepower and it is possible that, upon further investigation, additional power could be developed at special seasons. It is obvious, therefore, that an average of 1,100 horsepower could be obtained and if this power was disposed of as rated, it would yield an annual return of $26,400 or 1,100 horsepower at $2 per month. If an allowance of $6,000 is deducted for running expenses a net profit of $20,400 per annum would result. $20,400 capitalized at 10 per cent equals $204,000 the value of the power. The department is paying $20 per horsepower per annum for power. The valuation, then, was $150,000 Among the machinery there was one engine, practically new. I am not going to enter into any elaborate discussion with regard to the value of the property. My hon. friend values it at $200,000; plus a minimum of $150,000 in respect of the power we get $350,000. Then take the buildings. My hon. friend says that they have no practical utility for the purposes of the government. He also refers to the fact that the lease held by the government would enable the government to construct those buildings, or a portion of them, on the leased property -and that is only a part-without compensation. If he reads the clause in the lease he will see that the lessees have power of removal. I do not think anyone will argue seriously that this government or any other, or any individual, for that matter would attempt to drive the lessees to the position of removing the building. The valuations placed on the buildings by competent valuators are: In parcel No. 2, which my hon. friend who has had the details will perhaps understand better than the various other members of the committee, the valuation is $156,944; for parcel No. 3 the valuation is $219,311, and for parcel No. 4, $41,384. It is not necessary to go into details. These buildings are fireproof and are well constructed, and they are very suitable for the purposes for which the government intend to use them.

The reason I am asking the question is that at present I am sure he could ge.t a better -price for that property-namely $485,000, which is at the rate of $2,300 per foot.-than he will be able to get some time from now, because business is moving south on Ouellette avenue, and there is a boom in real estate there at present. The party who has offered that price for the property is, I understand, willing to lease it to the government for three years, or until the new building is erected, which I suppose will be on Canadian National property. since 1923, when Mr. Healy was a member of this house. He had an idea at that time about the new city 'hall, but I received a telegram from the mayor of Windsor yesterday as follows:
Present city hall site abandoned; council favours waterfront for post office.

these statements are incorrect, because there has been such a ballyhoo in connection with this post office that the people of Windsor are beginning to believe that the Minister of Public Works is not sincere at all. Mr, KENNEDY: Do I understand that this is the vote to provide salaries for the staff of the House of Commons? If so, I would like to ask a question in. connection with the members' stenographers staff. A petition was signed by about 165 or 175 members, and representations were made to the Speaker of the house, requesting an increase in the salaries of that staff. In view of those representations I would like to know if any increase has been decided upon, and if so, what?

I have received representations from the hon. gentleman and from two or three others who presented a petition on behalf of the staff. Every year I am met with the same request on the part of temporary employees in the service of the House of Commons. After receiving a delegation composed of the hon. gentleman and five or six other members of the house,
I promised to consult the secretary of the Civil Service Commission. I may say it would

be much more satisfactory to me if the whole service of the House of Commons was under the commission because, as I say, every year I am assailed by requests for salary increases. We have an excellent staff of stenographers. Some are paid $3.50 and others $4.50, and two chiefs receive $5, per day. Now, I cannot take upon myself to give an increase to all those employees, for I do not know their qualifications. I may say to the hon. gentleman that our stenographers receive on the average as much as, and in some cases more than, stenographers in the other departments receive. However, I have arranged with Mr. Smith, the very able director of the stenographic staff, to take this matter up with me after the session, and we will then see what can be done.

I cannot agree with Mr. Speaker's statement. I was asked to give the question some study by the members in this corner of the house. I have discussed the matter with the secretary of the Civil Service Commission,-
I have the correspondence.
-I asked him in what grade most of the stenographers would classify under the Civil Service Commission.
How does he know?

He said they would
mostly classify grade 2 and grade 3. I think it is possible for a grade 2 stenographer in the civil service to earn from $1,080 to $1,380 per annum, with two weeks holidays; and for grade 3 to earn from $1,380 to $1,620, or an average of about $1,500. Under the present conditions the earning of the stenographers must be about $1,200 per annum, or from $100 to $300 lower than the stenographers in other departments of the government who are doing approximately the same kind of work. The longer hours of work of the House of Commons stenographers must also be taken into account, running from seven to ten hours per week in excess of the hours in the other departments. It seems to me that the salaries of the stenographers of this house should compare with those received by the stenographers in the other departments. In my opinion we are voting salaries for the house stenographers that are lower than those paid to stenographers in the civil service doing the same kind of work, and if this is the case I think the Commons staff should be brought in line with the civil service staff generally.

Mr. Chairman, I
support the position taken by the member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy). The House of Commons stenographers are receiving a salary for only four or five months of each year, and when the session is over they have to try to find some other employment, which is not at all easy in July or August. I think they are perfectly justified in their demands for increased pay, and therefore I signed the petition.
I should like to ask His Honour through you, Mr. Chairman, if the report is correct that the salaries of the stenographic staff of the Senate have been raised.

There is no Senate Board of Internal Economy to consult with us. There are only five or six stenographers there. But to give the increase which has been requested on behalf of the stenographers by some hon. members would require an additional sum of $26,000. I have not the money.

I am astonished that
five or six stenographers in the Senate should receive an increase and the Commons stenographers should not. The work of the stenographers in the Senate is not to be compared with the work of those in the Commons. Because there, is a large numiber of stenographers is no reason why they should not be put on the same footing as the stenographers of the Senate.

If we add to that the expense of delegates to conferences, the travelling allowances of judges at fairs, the travelling allowances to persons making milk tests, the travelling expenses of purchasers of stock in car lots and the travelling expenses of delegates purchasing rams, we have a total of $876,638.39. If we add to that the cost of new automobiles, repairs and renewals, which comes under the head of travelling expenses, we have a total of $902,595.43. If my information is correct we could save a very considerable portion of that sum if we cut out some of this overlapping.
The estimates of the Department of Agriculture since the present minister took charge, as shown in the general estimates, have increased from $5,179,094.50 in 1921-22 to 88,217,025 in 1928-29, an increase of over 58 per cent. An ordinary business concern would not have any objection to an increase of that kind if they were attaining corresponding results, but that is not the case. According to the Bureau of Statistics the value of dairy products for the year 1920 was $288,836,093, while in 1926, it had dropped to 8249,710,000. The value of fruit production in 1921 was $45,262,788, and in 1926 it dropped to $21,611,379. The value of vegetable production including potatoes in 1921 was $108,047,600, while in 1927 it dropped to $80,241,56103-260
000. The value of farm eggs in 1921 was $40,968,841, and in 1927 that increased to $80,110,000. The number of sheep on farms in 1921 was 3,675,857, while in 1927 it was 3,262,700.
I am not going to take up the time of the house with any more of these figures, but it seems the more inspection we have the smaller our production comes, according to the figures I have given from the official returns.

Of course my hon. friend knows that the minister is absent, and he also knows that if the minister were 'here he would be quite capable of giving an effective answer to the figures and arguments produced by my hon. friend. I might point out, however, with respect to the overlapping which my hon. friend alleges, that already the inspection of seeds, feeds, fertilizers, insecticides, hay and twine are conducted by the same men, and there are many other instances where inspectors do two kinds of work. It is not technically possible in some cases to do so, however.

I would like to support the remarks of the hon. member for Wetas-kiwin with regard to this stock insurance. That condition has been very unsatisfactory in Canada. The farmer is charged the flat rate whether the stock are healthy or otherwise, and I think something should be done to better this condition.
I would like to ask the minister if he could give the committee any information as to the progress being made in experiments having to do with inoculation for the prevention of bovine tuberculosis?

It is almost eleven o'clock and we must make provision for going on later; therefore I move that the committee rise and report progress and ask leave to sit again this day.
Progress reported.

Your obedient servant,
James F. Crowdy,

I want to say

Many of the inspectors referred to are self sustained,
[Mr. Mackenzie King.j

The Auditor General's

I entirely agree with the
hon. gentleman that agriculture is a basic industry and we should vote all the money that is required and which will be properly spent, but my contention was that these inspectors were overlapping.
I must disagree with that.

Since the hon. member for Algoma West (Mr. Simpson) has brought up the question of government inspectors under the Department of Agriculture, I would like to read a short editorial which appeared recently in the Eastern Chronicle published in New Glasgow, Nova Scotia.
The Chronicle is owned and edited by James A. Fraser, one of the most influential Liberals in that province, and the opponent of the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Cantley) in the last election.
We will be very glad to have the hon. gentleman put it on Hansard, and we will take it as read.

On the Farm
Visitor:	Are those men I see about your
place, your hired men?
Farmer:	No, I have no hired men; those
men are government experts. That one in the barnyard attends to the health of the cows and

sees that they are kindly dealt with; he was sent here by Industrial relations, Halifax. That one down at the gate is there to prevent me selling any vegetables except by weight. I have no scales, hence do not sell any vegetables. Last summer I did quite a business selling early vegetables to wayfarers, but not having scales this year I did not sell any. The man you refer to was sent here by Hon. Mr. Motherwell, Ottawa. He has one on each farm, 9,000 of them altogether, so it is said. Oh, yes, that man over in the turnip field is Dr. Melville Cumming. His job is to prevent turnips from growing big, and to see that one of them does not grow bigger than the other. Not a bad fellow, Melville; but his head gets, at times, not lousy, but buggy, and then he cuts up as queer capers as any of them. But of all the ministers, the Minister of Agriculture has them all beaten. He has his experts, wherever a stalk of grain grows-thousands of experts. The other day in the House of Commons when Motherwell was on one of his particular frolics, all the opposition members were after him; among them Col. Cantley, who said to him, "If you go on as you are going, there won't be a Liberal farmer in Pictou County at the next election." "So much the better for you," retorted Minister Motherwell. As a rule, a political party could carry on if the half-baked fools they sometimes elect would act half wisely in parliament. Ministers like Motherwell would kill any government even if the angel Gabriel was Premier.

Had the Minister of Agriculture been here to-night and in charge of his estimates, I can assure you this item would not have passed. As he is absent we are perhaps in the position of being practically forced. I appreciate that the minister in charge of these estimates is not in a position to accept a reduction, and I do not wish to embarrass the government. I served notice on the Minister of Agriculture a week ago that when this item was before this house it was my intention to move that this item be reduced by $85,000, the amount that would be paid to A fairs. Perhaps it would be well to examine just why we are protesting against the action of the minister in this regard. As far as I know there is not an A class fair in Canada that has not a very large surplus.
Mr. FORIvE:	My hon. friend will pardon me, we have had a deficit at Brandon for years.

I think you will find that
most A class fairs have surpluses, and I venture to say there is not a B class fair that is not suffering deficits. In most cases the directors are carrying a personal responsibility in order to manage the institution. We are asking that the grant of $1,500 which we have been receiving for the last two years be continued. It seems rather strange, Mr. Chairman, that an industry producing several hundred of millions of dollars of wealth in this country cannot pay the small amount of $33,000 to supply a grant of $1,500 to twenty-two B class fairs. As a representative of
the riding of North Battleford, I must stand up in this house to-night and protest against the action of the Minister of Agriculture in taking the stand he has in connection with class B fairs in Saskatchewan and outside the province. I believe this is one of the biggest mistakes any Minister of Agriculture has ever made in the history of Canada. I cannot understand how any Minister of Agriculture

can take the stand that class B fairs ought to be wiped out, so far as grants are concerned. In the province of Saskatchewan $5,000 is granted to the class A fair in Saskatoon and another $5,000 to the class A fair in Regina. Instead of following the sensible policy of decentralization, one of centralization is followed, and that policy is never the real policy of Liberalism. I want to protest to-night, as the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ward) has protested, against eliminating these grants to class B fairs. I serve notice to-night, as a member from northern Saskatchewan that next year-*

No more
guns; do not tote any guns.

If the grants to class B fairs are not to be considered, the ones being made to class A fairs must be removed. There is a well defined public opinion in northern Saskatchewan, so far as the minister is concerned, that great pressure has been brought to bear upon him and his deputy and others in his department by the class A fairs to have this grant eliminated and the class A grant stand. The deputy minister shakes his head, but he can shake his head for a long time because that public opinion is well maintained, and, so far as I am concerned, I believe there is something in it.
Before taking my seat, I would like to give a few figures which were secured from the director of agricultural extension of the province. The average revenue for the years 1921-25 for the class A fairs-Regina and Saskatoon-was $38,158, and the average revenue for the same period for the Saskatchewan class B fairs was $4,264. The average entry fees for the same period foT class B fairs was $1,449, and for A fairs $3,166. The average amount received from concessions for the same period for B fairs was $1,867 and A fairs, $27,849. The average total for the class B fairs in Saskatchewan for that period was $7,581, and for class A fairs, $69,174. The average paid out in prizes for live stock in the class B fairs was $7,140 out of an average total of $7,581, or practically 100 per cent, while for the class A fairs there was paid out an average of $20,391 out of a total of $69,174, or barely 33 per cent. That shows the work the class B fair is doing in an agricultural way. They are the fairs of the farmers. The others are entirely different, and the reason I am standing up in the house to-night and defending the class B fairs is that I believe they are

doing a great work in the development of agriculture. They can give to the development of agriculture in Saskatchewan a great contribution that the class A fairs can never give. Therefore if the class B grants are to be discontinued, my remarks to-night will serve as notice to the Department of Agriculture that I am going to work tooth and nail until the grants for class A fairs are also eliminated, so that we shall have the two on a strict basis of equality and that is the only fair, just and equitable policy to pursue.

speechtext: May I recall to my hon. friend the fact that the first estimates taken up this session were those of agriculture? There were several discussions in the committee on the estimates of the Department of Agriculture.

I quite agree with the Prime Minister on that point, but we have only a few minutes to discuss the most important item of the whole estimates of that department. We can vote $18,000,000 for Defence. We can spend $300,000 on dredging in Ellis bay for a private company. We have a vote of only about $7,000,000 for agriculture and now we are cutting down on the best fairs we have in western Canada to which the young fellow can come along and put in an exhibit while, if he is cut out of that and has to go to the class A fair, he is too backward and bashful to put in an exhibit. I am in a very difficult position. I desire to expedite the business of the house and yet I must make certain observations with respect to this matter. I will endeavour to do so as briefly as possible because I am sure members of the committee are as desirous as I am to expedite the business, but I must make these observations. Yesterday evening the Minister of Railways said that it was essential that we should build a second hotel at Halifax in order to maintain the morale of the Canadian National employees.
I did not. The distinction is very important.

What is the distinction?
I will endeavour to read exactly what he said. The minister means that he was told

that that would be so. Is that what he
means?	[DOT]
My hon. friend had better read the exact language.

He says at page 4026 of Hansard:
Moreover, the president of the railway assures me, has assured me on more than one occasion, that the morale of the men engaged in working on the Canadian National system from cqast to coast would be seriously affected if the ' Canadian National were compelled to back down with respect to the construction of a Canadian National hotel at Halifax.
That statement is one that I think should not be seriously considered by this house in determining what action should be taken, for it is a statement that must be regarded as entirely at variance with what we know. The truth is that in 1926, not 1927, discussions took place between the president of the railway company and certain financiers in Halifax looking to the construction of a hotel. In February, 1927, Mr. Pratt wrote a letter, which I read last evening, in which he said that the president and directors were interested in this undertaking. That is clear. What is more, it subsequently develops that by reason of the very action that he then took, the Lord Nelson Hotel company was organized. The Dwyer property on which an option was taken in the fall of 1926 was acquired, and it was arranged to build an hotel upon it. That is beyond all question.
If my hon. friend will permit me, he mentions the option of 1926. That option had long since expired.
It had long since expired, but is was renewed for the purposes of the Lord Nelson hotel.
To be quite fair, my hon friend should state that the option of 1926 had no connection with what took place in 1927.
Oh yes.
It was an entirely new transaction in 1927.

It will be observed that the Canadian National Railway Company in their report of 1928 commence their observations with respect to the hotel by saying:
In 1926 a plan, which had been privately promoted for the erection of a modern hotel at Halifax, was presented to the board of directors for consideration. The plan was found to be unsatisfactory in its method of finance and was rejected. The need of more modern hotel facilities at Halifax was, however, apparent to the board, and it was recog-

nized that, with the establishment in the winter of 1928-29 of the new and important services of the Canadian National steamships between Halifax and the West Indies, this need would become still more pressing.
And it was in February, 1927, February, mark you, February 9, 1927, that Mr. Pratt wrote the letter which I read yesterday.
I was dealing only with the matter of the option, and I said that the option of 1926 had nothing to do with the purchase of 1927.
But there was a continuity with respect to the transaction.
There was no continuity; it was a brand new transaction. The site was not taken until October 17 or 18, 1927, and it was not inconsequence of the option of 1926.

That does not detract from what I am endeavouring to say. In the spring of 1927 the Canadian National indicated its interest in the undertaking of the construction of the hotel in Halifax, and when it is said that the morale of the road will be in some sense affected, let me say this. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company have made it perfectly clear that they will turn their stock over, as well as the $250,000, if the hotel wants it. So far as the Canadian Pacific Railway is concerned, they are prepared to back down and out and to disappear out of the transaction. The papers published all that. They had only $100,000 of preferred shares in the undertaking and in consequence of the Lord Nelson company being let down by the Canadian National, the Canadian Pacific took, it up.
I am going to point to one thing, in order that there may be no misapprehension. The report of the Canadian National Railways undertakes to indicate that the Canadian Pacific Railway did not care to take up the stock until September, 1928. It says on page 11 of its report:
The decision of the Canadian Pacific to take up tne preferred stock of the hotel company was made by the executive committee of that railway company three days later.
That is, three days after the Canadian National had determined to go into Halifax. That is not in accordance with the facts. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company, as the public records show, not their records at all, but two gentlemen whose word will be accepted in any court of law saw the president of the Canadian National, and he agreed to take the $250,000 and urged them to get the Canadian Pacific to take the $100,000.
My hon. friend said that the public records would prove it. What public records?

The records of the Lord Nelson Hotel Company, and the journey to Montreal of the president of that company, together with the delegation, which reported back, as was published in the press. What is more, the report of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company at page 7 says:
Your directors, after discussion with the National railways and upon the strong recommendation of the latter, agreed to subscribe for $100,000 of the preferred stock in the Lord Nelson hotel at Halifax. Nova Scotia, the National Railways undertaking to recommend the government's approval of a subscription by that company of $250,000 of such stock.
It is admitted by the speeches of the two ministers that that recommendation was made to the government. The government was dissatisfied with it, and it was not carried into effect by the shareholders, the shareholders being the governor in council. A new plan was submitted, but the government was not satisfied with that; the shareholders again disagreed. Then it was that the president of the Canadian National journeyed down upon a special train to the city of Halifax, and made a speech about predatory wealth, and the new hotel was recommended, the new Canadian National hotel. It was after that, that the Canadian Pacific agreed to take $250,000 of preferred stock, and it was then that the report of the Canadian National endeavours to make it clear that the agreement to take $250,000 of preferred shares referred to the whole $350,000, which is not so, and never has been so, because Mr. Silver, the chairman of the Lord Nelson hotel, accompanied the Premier of Nova Scotia and others to Montreal and arranged with respect to the $100,000 subscription of preferred shares by the Canadian Pacific. There should be no difficulty in understanding clearly that point.
One other question arose last evening. It was said last evening that the rebate of a commission that Mr. Bain and others agreed to was a rebate that went to the company, and it is not clear that that was money that went back to the company for work in Canada of the Lord Nelson Hotel Company.
There is no doubt about that.

I have received a telegram from the president of the company saying that the newspaper reports did not make it clear that that money was not for the purpose

of paying the promoters, but was to go back to the hotel to increase their working capital.
That is exactly what I said.

I just mention that in order to clear up any misapprehension that might arise from the press reports, in view of the telegram I have received. I desire to make it clear that such was not the case on the statement that has been made.
I can sum up this matter in this way. My hon. friend referred to the question of impressing this house with his influence. Let me put it this way: When the president of the Canadian National discovered that the minister from Nova Scotia was against the participation of the Canadian Pacific in the hotel, he did what any president would do. He said: Now is my chance to get an hotel, and I am going to get it on my own, and it was the position taken by the ministers in question that put this country to that expenditure. The president of the Canadian National is not to blame; the blame rests with the ministers, and not with the railway company at all, because in this instance an arrangement was made by the government to turn down the proposal to build the hotel, even though it involved a loss of $100,000 for one hotel, and to build a hotel solely for the Canadian National system.
The suggestion that has been made that we should build bungalow camps and hotels that will bring us a more profitable return is one that is worthy of consideration. In this regard I cannot hope to go over this matter in detail. It is sufficient for my purpose to say, and say clearly, that I protest against the investment of capital which involves an admitted loss of $100,000 per annum, according to the reports made by the Canadian National's own expert. The report of the company itself for last year shows that the company did not make interest on a single dollar of capital invested in hotels, but had a deficit in operating the whole hotel system of $15,000. Here are the * figures in that regard, to be found at page 8 of the Canadian National report:	It says that the losses had
been reduced to about $15,000, as compared with a loss of $35,000 for 1926. It is against this reckless waste of public money for the purpose of enabling a minister merely to control the situation in a province that I protest. I protest against it on behalf of the taxpayers who must find the money. Without going into details I have only this further to say. When the Vancouver hotel was brought up last night we had the tu quoque argument.

The Minister of Railways and Canals knows that the settlement was made because of promises by Mackenzie and Mann to the city of Vancouver under their agreement with the government in connection with the Canadian Northern British Columbia railway system, by which they were to build a hotel and do many other things involving an expenditure of millions of dollars. The settlement made by the Liberal government involved a vast expenditure of moneys in British Columbia and then the leasing of the hotel at a rental that would be sufficient to cover interest and sinking fund.

My hon. friend knows
better than that.

That is the arrangement
that was made. Mr. McCrossan, the city solicitor for Vancouver, came down here for the purpose, the arrangement was made and notified in the public press.

My hon. friend knows
perfectly well that the Minister of Railways consistently refused to recommend to his colleagues any such arrangement. It was never so recommended and never so authorized by this government. Where is the order in council authorizing it? My hon. friend says this government did something. There is one way by which governments do things.
Will my hon. friend just sit down?
Yes, and I will get up by and by.
Now, having sat down-

I merely want you to
speak the truth.

The hon. gentleman will
withdraw that statement, even at this late stage of the session.

That is right.

Haven't you been

Well, I thought the hon. gentleman the other day made admissions that were sufficiently serious for any of us in this house who understand the English language. Now, Mr. Chairman, I was proceeding to say that the Vancouver situation was a settlement of outstanding claims against the Canadian Northern Railway Company. Those claims involved this country in many millions of dollars. When the agreement was made for the building of an hotel it was signed and sent back to this city. The then Acting Minister of Railways (Sir Henry Drayton) at once had his attention directed to the fact that as the supply bill had not carried there was a question as to the legality of an appropriation by governor general's warrant to meet any possible claim there might be with respect to :he hotel. In other words, there was no parliamentary sanction with respect to the money that would enable the hotel to be built. That is the position with respect to that. I have no hesitation in saying that I pointed that out. It was subsequently discovered by the legal gentlemen connected with the department to be a correct statement of the situation. The contract was not signed. It was not proposed to sign it when that was found to be the condition. Then the statement was made that the hon. gentleman referred to last evening as to whether he desired to sign it himself. That is the reason I have made the protest, and if this house does not prorogue to-night I will have an opportunity to deal with it more fully on Monday, but in view of the desire to prorogue I shall make no further observations at the moment.

My hon. friend has made one statement with respect to the Vancouver hotel which, under the rules, I am not permitted to describe correctly. It has a bearing upon my association with the negotiations with the city of Vancouver prior to the dissolution of parliament in 1926, and it has also to do with what the shadow government then in office did or did not do in reference to an agreement to build an hotel in Vancouver.
My hon. friend stated in the plainest terms that the Liberal government had completed the arrangement. Those were his words.

That is what Mr. Mc-
Crossan, the city solicitor of Vancouver, said.
I sat down when my hon. friend requested it. Will he now kindly keep quiet?
I will see.

My hon. friend stated
in the plainest of terms-I find he stated it on the word of somebody else outside this house altogether-that the government did so and so. Apparently he does not yet know, or would pretend that he does not know, that any action of that sort by a government is represented by an order of council which is of record. He knows perfectly well that if a decision had been taken by this government to lease or build any hotel at Vancouver, that decision would be found in the records of the Privy Council. There is no such order in council. My hon. friend knew when he spoke that there was no such order.
He did not. Now, Mr. Chairman, that remark will have to be withdrawn.
Sit down.
No, that remark is unparliamentary, absolutely, under the rules. There may be no misapprehension about that. It might as well be realized even if this house does not prorogue to-night.
I await your ruling, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman
says he did not have knowledge, certainly his word must be accepted.

I will accept his word.
Of course I accept also the position in which he puts himself, that he knew-that is what he said-that a transaction had been completed by this government-

I said the transaction
had been.
That the transaction had been completed by this government; and now he says he did not know whether an order in council had been passed in respect to it.
I do not know yet.

Let me go further. I
trust I have cleared up that point. I have a particular interest in it, Mr. Chairman, for the reason that continuous and steady pressure

was brought to bear upon me as Minister of Railways and upon my colleagues by interested parties in the city of Vancouver on both sides of politics to complete the arrangements for the building and leasing of an hotel there. I never was satisfied with the arrangement, the government never was satisfied with the arrangement, and I never gave any encouragement to those promoting it that the government ever would approve it. My colleagues, every one, can confirm that. What followed when my hon. friends came into office? We have listened to a very ingenious explanation of a very extraordinary transaction from my hon. friend this evening. Suddenly the shadow government during the hundred days, in spite of the knowledge that my hon. friend says they had with respect to the illegality of financial transactions involving governor general's warrants-I say in spite of that fact, on the seventh day of August during that hundred days an order in council was passed authorizing the expenditure of three and a half million dollars of the money of this country on a hotel in Vancouver.
Hear, hear.

Passed by a government which, as my hon. friend stated to-night, knew perfectly well they had no authority to secure money by governor general's warrants for such purpose-nor indeed for any other purpose.
I did not say that.
Order.

No, I have a right to
deny a statement I did not make.
What did you say?

I said that a question
as to the legality of it arose, and it was subsequently reported by the legal gentlemen in charge that the decision was properly taken. That is what I said.

It is very strange, Mr. Chairman. My hon. friend now says that a question as to legality subsequently arose. I should like to ask how that government was doing business. Here is the order in council, very carefully and elaborately drawn up. Am I to presume it was not drawn up by legal officers, by someone who knew what the law was when it was being drawn up?
No, sir.

Are they to admit that they got someone to draw up an order in council for an expenditure of $3,500,000 with-

out finding out whether or not the transaction would be legal after it was adopted? What does the order in council say? After reciting the problem of the old arrangement between the Canadian Northern Pacific and Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann, which my hon. friend, by the way, stated correctly this evening-an arrangement which we inherited when the Canadian Northern Pacific became a part of the Canadian National system, a problem which everyone has been seeking to solve for some years past-after reciting that, I say, this order in council goes on to state:
That it is the opinion of the board of directors of the Canadian National Railway Company that, in view of the progress made by the Canadian National Railways in revenue receipts during the present year the whole cost of the construction of the proposed five hundred room hotel can be met from the estimates which were submitted to parliament at its last session and approved by the select standing committee on railways and shipping.
That statement is made in the order in council, and even if the estimates had been passed, which they were not, as my hon. friend indicates even if the estimates had been pased, that order in council discloses that the government passing it was willing to spend $3,500,000 for a hotel in Vancouver out of moneys voted by parliament for entirely different purposes.
Not at all.

That is the only conclusion we can come to. I had the privilege of placing these estimates before the select standing committee on railways and shipping at the session of parliament referred to, and I can say that the government of which I was then a member did not contemplate, nor did the management of the Canadian National Railways contemplate, the erection of an hotel out of the proceeds of these estimates. The matter was never discussed before that committee, never discussed in this parliament. The shadow government during the 100 days found the necessity, the political necessity- a word which my hon. friend is so fond of using-of rushing into a deal for the building of an hotel in the city of Vancouver. I say political! necessity-
It was never executed.

The agreement was never executed but this order in council was passed to authorize the execution of it. The government went as far as it could in authorizing execution by passing this document which I hold in my hand. The actual execution of it

was in the hands of the minister who is here authorized, and of the Canadian National management, who also are here authorized to proceed immediately with it and to take for the purpose $3,500,000 of money which this parliament voted for other purposes and not for the purpose of the Vancouver hotel. As my hon. friend would say, "That is the position with respect to that". I am speaking with some feeling, I admit.
Always do.

Yes, I am speaking with some feeling because my hon. friend to-night sought to fasten upon me an arrangement which I never consented to, always protested against, and refused to have anything to do with. In fact, so far from accepting it, this order in council passed by my .hon. friends opposite did not satisfy me and did not satisfy the government of which I am a member. I recommended the cancellation of it; my colleagues accepted that recommendation and it was cancelled. I will not go further into details as to what was contemplated as the result of this order in council. It is not an arrangement of which my hon. friend is personally proud, I know, and yet he was the finance minister of the government which authorized it by the document I hold in my hand.
Now with respect to the Halifax hotelhaving cleaned up Vancouver as well as I am able-with respect to the Halifax hotel I have just this to say. With regard to Vancouver the charge is made against me by hon. members opposite and by their press that I had cancelled this order in council- this order I had been referring to, passed by my hon. friends opposite-that I had cancelled it at the behest of the Canadian Pacific Railway because they had an hotel in Vancouver. Nay, it was further stated by gentlemen who sit opposite and by their friends, that I had been bribed by the Canadian Pacific Railway by having an hotel built by them in the city which I have the honour to represent. That was published broadcast through the press of western Canada, at least that portion of the press willing to publish that sort of thing.
Were they sued for libel?

They were not sued for
libel. I-well, I guess I had better not say it; I will stay within the rules. Now, the estimates presently under consideration by the house, recommended by Sir Henry Thornton and the management of the Canadian National Railways, include an amount of $100,000 towards the construction of an hotel in Vancouver. I can tell my hon. friends it will not be constructed on the plan they devised; it will be constructed in a business-like way. Now reverse the situation and let us go to Halifax. There my hon. friend is seeking to prevent the Canadian National from building an hotel. May I ask, is he acting in the interests of the Canadian Pacific Railway, as I was accused by his party of doing when I did what was my public duty in regard to the Vancouver matter? My hon. friend has himself on occasion, when I have taken a position with respect to the department and its affairs, intimated somewhat sneeringly that I am working in the interests of the Canadian Pacific Railway.

Name me an instance
when that was said.

My hon. friend frequently did during last session. I am within the memory of the house, and my hon. friend will find it in Hansard of last session. It was possibly intended as persiflage, but not of a very pleasant kind.
You will not find it in the records of the house. I have said it to you personally on the street when we have walked down.

My hon. friend might
search Hansard; I will help him. If he does he will find something which he would not like to see.
If personal observations of that kind are repeated in the house, well and good.

Be that as it may, all that I said last night with respect to the Halifax hotel stands to-day. I believe that Sir Henry Thornton is right when he says that whatever may happen to the other hotel the Canadian National hotel at Halifax will develop business and will ultimately succeed. To-night my hon. friend stressed the supposed loss of $100,000 a year which may be incurred in operation on the Canadian National hotel system. If we take his remarks seriously at all he must be arguing that therefore we should not build or own hotels. But he is too wise for that in reality; he knows that the value of a hotel to a railway system does not depend upon the earnings of that hotel but that it has a relation to the traffic handled by the railway. All our hotels are great traffic producers for the

road, and although on paper they may lose money in operation, they more than make it up in the contribution they make to the general well-being of the system, and I believe the Halifax hotel will be no exception in this regard.

I just want to say one word in order to put my hon. friend right in the matter of dates. ELe has suggested tonight that the subscription of the Canadian Pacific Railway was made before the announcement by the Canadian National Railways.
Not the whole subscription, but $100,000 of it.

Well, the whole or any part of it. I want to say to my hon. friend that if he will look at the record he will find that on July 6, the Lord Nelson Hotel Company advertised in the Halifax Herald, and in that newspaper appeared a letter signed by H. R. Silver, president, in which it is stated:
It is confidently expected that in the event of Canadian National Railway Company purchasing this amount of preference shares, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company will also subscribe for $100,000 par value of the preference shares on the same terms.
The Canadian National Railway Company did not subscribe, and I want to tell my hon. friend that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company did not subscribe at that time. On July 14 the announcement was made which I read to the house last night, to the effect that I felt satisfied in my own mind that the item would be placed in the estimates if the management of the railway recommended it. On July 20, Sir Henry Thornton stated that the board of directors of the company would put this item in the estimates, and not until September 26, over two months later, did the Canadian Pacific Railway announce having taken up that subscription. That announcement is contained in the Halifax Chronicle of September 28, in a letter from Mr. Beatty under date of September 26 to Mr. H. R. Silver which has the following to say:
Our executive committee to-day approved a subscription by this company to the preferred stock of the Lord Nelson hotel to the amount of three hundred and fifty thousand dollars par value, conditional upon the bonds and balance of preferred stock being sold.
Let that settle the matter of dates. The Canadian National Railways made their announcement on July 20 and the Canadian Pacific subscription and announcement were

made on September 26, so when my hon. friend suggests that a portion of the subscription was taken up before he is palpably in error.
He is seeking to blame the minister; for what? I have told him the reason why this proposition was turned down; one reason was because it was too expensive. I quote the statement made by my hon. friend last night, in which he said:
That in my judgment was a proper view to take, having regard to the fact that the commission to be paid was much larger than should be paid for securing capital under these circumstances.
The other reason was that parliament had not authorized that expenditure, which was commended by my hon. friend. I do not know how he blames the ministers under those circumstances. The proposition was turned down on July 14 and immediately after that the announcement was made. I think with this matter of dates straightened out the house will have no difficulty in coming to a conclusion on the argument made by my hon. friend.
The only difficulty about it is that the statement of the bon. gentleman with respect to dates is not borne out by the record. Would my hon. friend mind reading the exact words of that letter again?

This is what I read:
It is confidently expected that in the event of Canadian National Railway Company purchasing this amount of preference shares the Canadian Pacific Railway Company will also subscribe for one hundred thousand dollars par value of the preference shares on the same terms.
The other letter, from Mr. Beatty, was as follows:
Our executive committee to-day approved a subscription by this company to the preferred stock of the Lord Nelson hotel to the amount of three hundred and fifty thousand dollars par value, conditional upon the bonds and balance of preferred stock being sold.
And the date?
September 26.
Previously the company had agreed to invest $100,000. Now I will read from the statement of the president.
I am giving the statement made by the Lord Nelson Hotel Company.

Your directors, after discussion with the National Railways and upon the strong recom-

Nova Scotia, the National Railways undertaking to recommend the government's approval of a subscription by that company of $250,000 of such stock. I am taking the public announcement.
Mr. Silver confidently expected it in July, and his expectation was realized. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company agreed to subscribe $100,000.

My hon. friend will not
find any agreement to subscribe $100,000 after July.

Does my hon. friend say
that they never agreed to subscribe $100,000?
Yes, on the authority of Mr. Silver.

Yes.

No doubt that is where
Mr. Silver got his expectations.

He was surrounded by
witnesses who went up as a delegation. The Canadian Pacific did not want to go into this venture, but the Canadian National urged them to, and they did it for the sake of Nova Scotia as a whole. It says so. There is a

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This resolution involves an increase in salary for an official who comes under the Civil Service Act, and is subject to all the regulations of that act. I have nothing to say against this official, but I submit that if we are to permit officials whose case has been reviewed by the Civil Service Commission to go over the heads of the commission and of the treasury board and come to parliament, we are introducing a precedent which may have very far-reaching effects. On these grounds, Mr. Speaker, 1 submit that this resolution should not pass. Indeed I question whether it is in order.

The motion is not in
order, nor is the report, because a committee can take cognizance only of matters which are referred to it. The matter which is the subject of recommendation in this report was not referred to the committee by the house. In addition to that, the official referred to is an employee of the House of Commons and I was not consulted1 in the matter. The permanent employees of the House of Commons are under the Civil Service Commission, and the case of this excellent employee was reviewed by that commission. I regret to say that they did not find that he should get an increase, and then he went over my head and put the matter before the joint committee of both houses on the printing of parliament. I rule that the motion is not in order.

In justice to the committee I would say that this report has been 
adopted by the Senate, and we find ourselves in the peculiar position of having a report adopted by one house and rejected by the other. This official is paid out of the general vote for the printing of parliament. He has had no increase since 1915, and the committee recommended that he be placed in a higher class.
